These modes can be categorized into a high Adverse R-parity even-even type and a high Adverse R-parity odd-odd state. We investigate the existence and characteristics of these modes within a R-parity mixed system using a mathematical model that describes two rotors. We also explore how these modes can be identified through the R-parity even-odd transition matrix elements.

A new cell-mean based neural network method is proposed to solve hyperbolic and parabolic partial differential equations in a generalized form. This method employs local polynomial averages to utilize neighboring cell data within a spatial context. By incorporating neural networks, we approximate the time derivative using network outputs and their corresponding inputs from the spatial and temporal domains. This method exhibits high resistance to oscillations, as well as an adaptability to varying equation types, whether linear, nonlinear, sharp-fronted, smooth, hyperbolic, parabolic, or stiffly stiff. Additionally, we analyze the stability of this method through a von Neumann analysis for linear equations. Furthermore, we evaluate the method using representative examples, including 1D linear and nonlinear equations, 1D/2D/3D hyperbolic problems, 1D/2D/3D parabolic problems, and a Moyal equation.

The ALICE collaboration is working to upgrade ALICE with the primary goal of
improving particle detection capabilities and increasing run efficiency. The
upgrade, which is being planned for implementation after LHC Run 3, will enable
the experiment to reach its full potential in terms of data collection. This
will be done by integrating various detectors and systems, including the upgraded
muon spectrummeeter, which will significantly enhance the experiment's ability to
identify specific particles and measure related physics. The ALICE upgrade will
also include the development of a new muon detector and other systems, which
will significantly enhance the experiment's capabilities and capabilities for
data collection.

The Unruh effect describes how an accelerating detector perceives the Minkowski vacuum as a thermal state. Traditionally, this phenomenon is studied through detectors interacting with Minkowski space while in a constant acceleration. In a novel approach, we examine the Unruh effect from a different perspective, where the Minkowski observer is the accelerating one. In this scenario, the detector interacts with the light cones, separating time into past and future parts. Our research reveals the emergence of a non-trivial geometric phase in the detector's state, which can be measured experimentally by assessing the entanglement between time's past and future parts, utilizing time bin entanglement and homodyne detection techniques in optical interferometry experiments.

We are introducing a multilingual data set called MEE, focusing on machine
reading comprehension with three key multilingual languages: English, French,
and Spanish. The MEE data set is designed for incident detection and includes
over 12,000 carefully compiled documents. Our MEE data set is accessible at
https://github.com/robertomg1/MEE.

We derive and prove a global version of the Grothendieck-Riemann-Roch theorem, which takes into consideration a specific cohomology theory based on global cohomology spaces. This generalization relies on a novel form of the Grothendieck-Riemann-Roch formula applicable to morphisms between schemes of arbitrary dimensions that need not be proper. In addition, we explore its implications for characteristic properties of vector bundle morphisms and develop a proof of Andreatta's theorem on the positivity of Chern classes for geometric applications in algebraic geometry and string theory.

Our analysis of the stellar interplay in the hard X-ray state of Cyg X-1 reveals that the Comptonization of both accreted and emitted photons from the stellar wind and disk thermal radiation play crucial roles. The model developed incorporates a two-stage Comptonization process, where a stellar interplay and a more dense and larger wind contribute to the X-ray spectrum. Additionally, a set of parameters derived from a specific radiative transfer model for the stellar wind also fits the data well, although it is found that the primary contribution to the spectrum comes from the first Comptonization component. The model parameters obtained confirm earlier findings of significant wind contribution and a high electron temperature. The model also provides a more detailed understanding of the variability and the connection between X-ray and radio emission in Cyg X-1.

The study of a specific ether-like modification of a non-abelian gauge theory in both classical and quantum forms, especially at non-zero temperatures, is a critical task. In a gauge theory with the ether-like term, various aspects, such as classical vacuum configurations, thermal stability in a non-abelian gauge theory, and the calculation of the 1-loop thermal effective potential, are examined in a non-abelian gauge theory. In a non-abelian gauge theory, a non-zero value for the ether-like term can break Lorentz and gauge symmetries. In a non-abelian gauge theory, introducing specific ghost and anti-ghost kinetic terms, as well as a non-abelian ghost kinetic term, are required to address quantization issues. In a non-abelian gauge theory, introducing additional ghost and anti-ghost interaction terms, as well as a non-abelian ghost interaction term, are required to address the non-perturbative aspects of the quantum theory. In a non-abelian gauge theory, introducing ghost and anti-ghost interaction terms, as well as a non-abelian ghost interaction term, are required to address ghost mode issues. In a non-abelian gauge theory, ghost mode analysis reveals that the ghost mode mass depends on a non-abelian gauge coupling. In a non-abelian gauge theory, ghost mode analysis reveals that the ghost mode mass depends on the non-abelian gauge coupling. In a non-

Our approach to universal parsing combines two key components - the syntactic structure and the semantic representation - into a unified parsing process that requires no further task-specific training.  The semantic component is based on Meaning Extractor using 3-level type-validated semantic triples.  The syntactic component is based on STEREP using abstract syntax trees.  The semantic meaning is integrated into the syntax parser using two different methods, resulting in SMP1 and SMP2.  The SMP1 approach incorporates the Meaning Extractor dependency graph into the Stanford parser's feature set, while SMP2 uses the independently computed semantic meaning from SMP1 and re-validates it during decoding.  The results show that combining both components improves decoding performance, particularly for SMP2 which re-validates the semantic meaning.

We utilize the magnetized-cooling protocol originally developed by Kiuchi et al. (2018) to investigate post-merger dynamics following a neutron star binary collision. Our research examines how the size and magnetic field strength of the initial coalescing remnant impact the measurement of gravitational waves, with a particular focus on the neutron star's properties. We discovered that the size of the remnant varies significantly, typically falling within a range of 500-1200 meters, and exhibits a correlation with the size of the merged object and the initial size of the merged object. Our study highlights the importance of the magnetic properties of the neutron star in driving the post-merger outflows, with a peak in the Gravitational Wave spectrum observed at a frequency of 2.6 kHz for a specific set of parameters. Our results show that the size of the hot spot in the neutron star plays a pivotal role in the post-merger outflows, with a peak in the Gravitational Wave spectrum observed at a frequency of 2.6 kHz for a merged object with a mass of approximately 2.7 solar masses. Our study demonstrates that the size of the neutron star is influenced by the initial size of the merged object and the magnetic properties of the neutron star, with a peak in the Gravitational Wave spectrum observed at a frequency of approximately 2.6 kHz for a merged object with a mass of approximately 2.7 solar masses.

Early-type galaxies (ETGs) are known to harbor substantial dormant gas and stars resulting from past and ongoing tidal processes.
Using the High-Scalability Survey for Star-forming Galaxies data from Suprime-Cam, we found that a significant portion of the mass in the local universe is contained in these giganantic ETGs.
By separating tidal features from their parent galaxies, we discovered that these ETGs possess an approximately 10% fraction of their mass in these features.
Our findings suggest that a substantial portion of the mass in the local universe is contained in these tidal features.
Moreover, we found that a significant percentage of local galaxies are involved in ongoing tidal interactions.
Moreover, our research suggests that the local universe contains a significant percentage of stars that are currently being formed.
Moreover, our findings suggest that the mass loss rate of these ETGs is substantial and that they are likely to continue to lose mass in the future.
Moreover, our research suggests that the mass loss rate of these ETGs is similar to that of other galaxy types and that they are likely to continue to lose mass in the future.

A theoretical paper explores bipolar supermassive stars using the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation, revealing an anti-gravity effect that can trigger instability and potentially explain observed bipolar stellar phenomena, including those from massive binary systems, stellar clusters, and nebulae.

We have conducted an in-depth analysis of 11 confirmed Fast Radio Burst sources, including seven of our own discoveries, utilizing the CHIME radio telescope and the VLT optical facility with the X-shooter spectrograph. Our comprehensive search for optical counterparts and transient events in the vicinity of these sources has yielded no new findings. The existing constraints on optical afterglows and bursts are now more stringent than prior studies by a factor of about 100. Based on our results, we have established new limits on the synchrotron self-compton emission model in the X-ray to GeV energy range, thereby restricting the size of the emitting region to about 1000 times the Schwarzschild radius. Furthermore, we have found that the radio to optical light curve contrast is limited to approximately 10 to the power of 7.9. These findings have been used to further refine the "crustal star" and "black hole" models for the origin of FRBs, as well as to provide new limits on the magnetic reconnection model.

High-power laser technology is essential for cutting-edge manufacturing processes, cutting, welding applications, as well as cutting-edge laser applications like inertial fusion and advanced quantum technology. This thesis develops design methods and techniques for high-power laser systems across all these categories and employs optimization methods to enhance their performance. Moreover, it employs network-based approaches to efficiently explore and improve complex optical setups. Firstly, we address the requirements and design considerations of industrial lasers and develop design tools to efficiently evaluate and compare various design options. Secondly, we examine key design aspects of 3D printing technologies and employ an optimization method to evaluate and enhance existing laser setups and experimental arrangements for quantum simulations. Finally, we present a systematic approach to leverage and refine existing high-power laser designs using network representations and demonstrate its applicability to cutting-edge laser applications like inertial fusion and quantum simulation.

Current language models are being utilized in various ways to comprehend and describe images, but it is not possible for them to see and react to observed elements, only to see and describe images. Our study introduces a new method of integrating visual controls into text generation models to enable them to perceive and respond to real-world situations. By combining this method with existing language models, we can create versatile systems that can be deployed in areas such as human-robot interaction and game development, allowing these systems to adapt to user commands and instructions. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of this method by training it on a large dataset of annotated images and fine-tuning it on a smaller dataset with specific task-related goals. The resulting model achieves impressive accuracy on visual and spatial tasks, reaching 94% and 91% respectively, and can also be used in real-world scenarios to control a robot's movements and actions.

We present an innovative modification to existing RingCT, allowing users to delegate verification responsibilities to the payment processor by verifying a digital signature instead of the proof itself. We developed DRVC, a novel DRVC protocol that combines payment processor assistance with processor honesty assumptions to guarantee secure and efficient transactions. Our driving objective is to accelerate DRVC processing speed, making it more appealing for cryptocurrency adoption. Based on this concept, we developed DRVD, a more efficient and scalable payment protocol with enhanced resilience against processor malice.

A comprehensive study of beam brightness scans for beam diagnostics, building upon previous work, has been conducted. The impact of various factors on brightness scans and beam sizes was analyzed, including beam types, normalization methods, coordinate systems, and sigma-nesting conventions across simulation and diagnostic codes. The results of brightness scans can provide valuable insights into fundamental beam characteristics, including any changes that occur due to beam manipulation.

This research focuses on the data-driven modeling approach using data collected from a computer network, where each device functions as an individual node. An essential requirement of this method is the ability to handle high-dimensional data, which is typically characterized by short time series and high-dimensional feature sets. Utilizing a computational grid allows the local models to be trained in parallel on each node, with the goal of an accurate reconstruction of the target variable. However, a primary challenge lies in determining the optimal distribution of the target variable across the nodes. To overcome this limitation, a method involving the distribution of specific data features is introduced, along with techniques for combining these features on a central server. Experimental results, involving the task of energy consumption forecasting, have demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach, with a notable improvement in performance when the distribution of specific data features is used, compared to equal target variable allocation.

This paper examines the decay of the $\Upsilon(10753)$ into $\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ where $n$ is 1, 2, or 3. It uses the hadronic loop mechanism to analyze its transition process and explains why its decay width into $\Upsilon(4S)\pi^+\pi^-$ is larger than its decay width into $\Upsilon(2S)\pi^+\pi^-$, despite the latter having a larger phase space. Additionally, this paper predicts the decay width of the $\Upsilon(10753)$ into $\Upsilon(1S)\pi^+\pi^-$ and compares it with experimental results from BESIII, demonstrating that its predictions align with those results.

This study proposes a novel optimization technique called AskewSGD to efficiently train quantized neural networks with limited weight ranges. The proposed method is virtually unaffected by the non-differentiable nature of the quantization process and can be integrated into existing stochastic gradient descent methods with minimal changes. The experiments conducted on state-of-the-art interval-restricted optimisation baselines demonstrate that AskewSGD surpasses them by up to 6.4% in terms of top-1 accuracy while requiring no increase in training time. The implementation of AskewSGD is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/abhi12dev/AskewSGD.

This article presents a comprehensive overview of the techniques used to
utilize neural networks to generate the actuation patterns for soft robots.
These methods, known as model-driven approaches, differ from data-driven
techniques in that they do not heavily rely on large datasets to establish a
connection between a robot's inputs and outputs. Model-driven methods can be
further classified into three categories: physics-based, geometric-based, and
kinematic-based. Each category utilizes neural networks to solve specific
model-based problems. The first class employs soft robotics principles to
create robotic behaviors, the second focuses on topological transformations,
and the third addresses kinematic issues. The article begins with an
introduction to the fundamental concepts of model-driven methods and their
distinction from data-driven methods. It then provides an in-depth analysis of
the existing literature on model-based methods, including challenges and
future research directions.

This study is based on the premise that the Jacobi group Jab is authentically composed of the semi-direct product of the Kronecker group J and the Heisenberg group he, both of which are key components. We provide a novel proof for this assertion, building from the fact that Jacobi space jab is formed by the direct sum of the Heisenberg space he and the Kronecker space J, in an authentic manner.

The primary goal of fact checking with tabular data is to verify the authenticity of a given table statement. Nevertheless, current methods for fact checking with tabular data often struggle due to the complexity of the tables involved. As complex tables grow in size, the table's structure and semantic meaning can interfere with one another. Therefore, we introduce the concept of "disassembly" for tabular fact checking, which we define as the process of breaking down a complex table into smaller, simpler tables to verify their accuracy. These smaller tables can then be combined to derive the final table's meaning. To facilitate the study of disassembly, we created the first "disassembly" dataset, which requires models to identify the individual tables构成 of a complex table based on its raw data and image. Our results show that the proposed disassembly strategy significantly improves fact checking accuracy as the complexity of the tables increases, especially for tables with intermediate complexity levels, where we observe a notable improvement of over 8% in model accuracy.

Recent advances in general-purpose generative models, particularly in their ability to produce high-quality samples, have been significant, particularly with state-of-the-art generative adversarial networks. However, controlling these models in terms of specific attributes has been a challenge. This paper presents new methods for incorporating conditional information into the loss function of generative adversarial networks by parameterizing condition information within a shared latent space. These techniques enable the integration of one-hot vectors and continuous values, supported by novel support vector machines and regression models that operate in a margin or in a low-dimensional space, respectively. The experiments demonstrate the efficacy of these methods in high-quality image generation and successful control, surpassing previous approaches.

The nested sampling algorithm has been proposed in order to combine Bayesian computation and model evaluation under a single algorithm. One of its key components is the step selector that determines how many live points to use in the algorithm. This paper compares four step selectors that have been previously suggested. The nested sampling algorithm was run on different problems with various levels of complexity in order to assess its performance. The goal of the analysis was to understand the effects of each step selector on the analysis and to identify which one yields results closest to those of full nested sampling for a given number of live points. The outcome of the study revealed that the step selector developed by Dykstra and Thompson exhibits the full nested sampling results with the fewest live points possible.

For any connected graph, a fault-free distance labeling is a way to efficiently compute the shortest path distance between any two nodes in the presence of no node failures. Each node receives a unique label, and distances between nodes can be calculated by taking the absolute difference between their labels. Researchers previously found certain classes of graphs, such as outerplanar and series-parallel graphs, to allow for compact distance labeling, but these classes have a shared characteristic: they can easily be represented as a tree-like structure. We developed an algorithm that can label any planar graph using a small amount of space, approximately 14n bits for a graph with at most n nodes. Our algorithm allows distance calculations with at most four failures, achieving this compact distance labeling in a way that outperforms previous bounds that required Ω(n²) bits.

In this work, we examine the time-domain behavior of pair correlations for Bose-Hubbard models in one- and two-dimensional settings, subject to linear driving and damping forces. By utilizing an exact solution method to determine the system's time-domain behavior within the two-particle reduced density matrix, we map the model to an equivalent non-linear harmonic oscillator and compute its Green's function in the frequency domain, enabling a time-domain analysis of correlation functions via Fourier transformation. Our focus is on comparing the characteristics of pair correlation functions in both time and space domains with their steady-state spatial counterparts. By analyzing the peaks of pair correlation functions, we investigate how the effects of pairing within correlated pairs are influenced by parameters in both driven-damped systems and non-linear harmonic oscillators.

Solving a generalised version of Poisson's equation with boundary conditions and a specific mathematical structure, we find that a current must exist within $L^2$ on a compact manifold with the measure defined by the manifold's properties and a constant measure defined by the manifold's density. This equation involves a quadratic form defined within $L^2$ with currents, and we study a particular class of problems with this mathematical structure, and we find connections with several fields, namely mathematical physics, geology, and image processing. Our main tool is an adapted version of Fichera's work, along with the Hahn-Banach theorem.

In various domains, such as autonomous driving and robotics, identifying unexpected scenarios is critical. While existing Gaussian Process models can effectively analyze and learn from data within their domain, they often struggle to recognize new, unseen data. To address this issue, we propose a novel method called Distributional Gaussian Processes Strata (DGPS), which integrates the modeling of probability distributions with traditional Gaussian Processes to create a more effective framework for distinguishing between known and unknown data. By combining the power of distributional Gaussian Processes and strata, DGPS can learn the domain it was trained on and, in turn, identify out-of-distribution data. Our approach is shown to outperform state-of-the-art methods in several benchmark datasets for out-of-distribution detection.

In recent years, there has been a surge of interest in exploring non-equilibrium phenomena in driven quantum systems that are far from thermal equilibrium states. One notable aspect of these states is their unique stability against thermal heating. Previous attempts to observe such states experimentally have been challenging due to a variety of factors, but recent breakthroughs have led to the observation of non-thermal states. Nevertheless, the influence of thermal noise on these non-thermal states remains poorly understood. Our research demonstrates that in an open, optically-driven lattice system, the presence of an absorptive reservoir with the ability to remove photons from specific modes can protect the many-body non-thermal state from thermal noise. The unique characteristics of this absorption process allow for the control of heating rates, ultimately leading to the emergence of Bose condensation within the non-thermal state. Our approach offers a new method for controlling quantum states and opens up new avenues for studying thermal noise within Floquet states.

We establish a paper focusing on the H\"older continuity properties of solutions for the Monge-Amp\`ere equation with a bounded right-hand side, considering both convex and concave cases. Notably, in the concave scenario, we introduce an enhanced principle that improves the Alexandrov maximum principle and the second-order regularity by providing H\"older continuity for $\big\vert\det D^2u\big\vert$.

A clock signal's stability is crucial for making accurate measurements with optical clocks, but the time-domain methods used to measure stability are typically designed for stationary signals with regular patterns. This is not the case for optical clocks, which have time-varying signals due to the random nature of photons and the irregular spacing of absorption peaks in frequency combs. As a result, the standard methods for assessing stationarity lead to suboptimal results for optical clocks, and new statistical tools are needed. In this context, the paper outlines a set of statistical indicators to evaluate the time-varity of clock signals, including the autocorrelation function, power spectral density, and higher-order statistics, and demonstrates their application to typical optical comb signals and others used in optical clocks.

In Service Function Chain (SFC)-based Software Defined Networking (SDN), maintaining quality of experience for end users is heavily reliant on ensuring the quality of network services provided by various network functions. However, due to unexpected failures, preventive measures, and varying traffic demands, guaranteeing this quality is a constantly changing challenge. The centralization of control in SDN allows for swift and efficient utilization of network resources across different fog data centers, enabling flexible restoration of SFCs after disruptions. To tackle these issues, we propose JF-ESFC, a fog-supported, real-time SFC approach that restores failed and prevents over failure of SFCs through the joint optimization of fault modeling, reliability, and energy efficiency. Our simulation results show that JF-ESFC effectively restores SFCs after disruptions, significantly reducing energy consumption compared to existing solutions.

The choice of loss function significantly impacts the effectiveness of neural network training. Researchers, however, typically select it based on experience rather than theoretical principles, often prioritizing symmetry and monotonicity but neglecting the functional form, resulting in the common adoption of the hinge loss. This study utilizes "gradient surgery" to investigate the effects of various loss functions with a focus on those possessing symmetric and monotonic properties, and through experiments across multiple datasets, it is demonstrated that the specific loss function used can indeed make a notable difference in the performance of deep neural networks. This difference in performance is observed to be relatively minor within a certain category of loss functions but can be substantial when comparing different categories.

A novel class of 1D quantum circuits called Hyper-Invariant MERA is introduced, approximately supporting 1D quantum information theory's holographic error correction code. By leveraging its power-law symmetry, this class of circuits has an extensive, 0-dimensional effective description, making it amenable to efficient classical simulations. Approximately supporting the holographic error correction code allows these circuits to exhibit a efficient way of accounting for entanglement in the system, giving rise to interesting properties of quantum circuits. Additionally, the authors demonstrate that these 1D circuits can be constructed to approximate optimal area laws by leveraging its efficient description.

The Galactic Center's filaments hold significant mystery, but recent research has shed light on their general population. This study, which involved 143 filaments identified in 14 GC's 10kpc fields, analyzed the spacing between filaments and their positions. It was discovered that the median projected length of GC's filaments is 1.85 parsecs, with a population population filament spacing of 0.73 parsecs. Furthermore, the population filament density of the Galactic Center is 143 per 100 square parsecs.

A new approach to the Conservation Voltage Decrease (CVD) problem is proposed.
The CVD is an energy conservation measure that involves reducing voltages
below the recommended standards. We present a distributed algorithm that
lowers voltages across Primary-Secondary distribution systems to achieve a
specified energy savings target. Our algorithm considers the complexities
arising from transformer tap changers and ensures optimal performance even
with an increase in system scale. To achieve this goal, a semi-disaggregated
model construction is utilized, where a central level determines tap settings
and local levels calculate optimal on-load tap changer (OLTC) positions.
The model can be efficiently solved using advanced optimization techniques
based on semi-algebraic geometry and linearization methods.

In the non-stochastic bandit setting, we investigate a scenario involving an extended advisor who chooses arms with only partial knowledge, where only the reward for the selected arm is known to the advisor when it's made. The arm's reward remains unknown to the advisor until after the given time step. We consider the case in which any arm can be selected and focus on settings where only one arm's reward is actually known at each time step. Under these conditions, we develop both "best-of-two" and "target regret" measures to compare the advisor and non-stochastic bandit performer (NBFP) regrets to a specific benchmark. 

We develop and analyze two novel algorithms - "fully-observable" and "target-tracking" - and show that both are successful under certain conditions. Specifically, we show that "target-tracking" minimizes target regret up to a factor of $\kappa$, while "fully-observable" minimizes both target and NBFP regrets up to a factor of $\kappa^2$. In addition, we show that under certain conditions, any algorithm cannot avoid a certain level of regret without additional information, specifically a co-observability number.

Current text-generation techniques, including transformation-based models and recurrent neural networks, excel in creating coherent text but often fall short in replicating natural, human-like dialogue. A novel knowledge-transfer approach has been developed to produce more human-like dialogue by integrating both existing and newly acquired knowledge, including lexical, syntactic, and semantic models. These models, trained through large datasets, can be applied to generate realistic dialogue, as evidenced by their exceptional performance in an established benchmark. Additionally, the framework's capabilities were tested in an extended dialogue setting, showcasing its versatility and practical application across various domains.

This talk will examine lattice Qcd under conditions of non-zero temperature and density, discussing how these simulations are conducted and presenting findings from my research on the Nambu--Jona-Linino phase transition.

A key method for reducing the use of offshore wind turbines while improving reliability involves applying probabilistic fatigue load modeling. This model generates realistic hourly load distributions from which specific stress quantiles can be extracted, enabling probabilistic availability assessment. Although traditional methods relying on Monte-Carlo simulations are effective, they are highly computationally expensive. To address this limitation, researchers have proposed using Gaussian Process regression to create surrogate models. However, these models have significant limitations, primarily their assumption of Gaussian stress distributions, which is often inaccurate. To overcome this limitation, a new approach has been developed that can accurately fit non-Gaussian distributions. This approach involves using Gaussian Process regression to model individual stress components (mean, standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis) based on available turbine data, such as wind speed and time. The resulting model can accurately predict the mean and standard deviations of the turbine's fatigue load. The accuracy of this model has been validated by comparing the quantiles of the predicted and true distributions. The results show that the model can accurately predict the stress quantiles of the turbine's fatigue load, with a significant reduction in computational cost compared to traditional methods.

In this research paper, we explore the dynamic nature of the Twitter social network through the analysis of the 2023 Izmir earthquake. By employing computational tools, we examine how users reacted to and shared information about the disaster in real-time. Our study examines various network characteristics, including user interactions, conversation spread, and user behavior. By measuring metrics such as in-degree, out-degree, in-strength, out-strength, in-out-degree difference, in-out-strength difference, in-degree correlation coefficient, out-degree correlation coefficient, in-strength correlation coefficient, out-strength correlation direction, and input data sets, we identify patterns and relationships within the network. Our findings reveal the role of Twitter as a platform for real-time disaster response and information exchange.

We demonstrate that certain families of nilpotent quotients of generalized Baumslag-Solitar groups exhibit the R_infinity property, whereas others do not, depending on their specific group action parameters.

A new approach is developed in this research to invert complex dynamical systems from incomplete data, particularly those exhibiting chaotic behavior. This method is rooted in optimal control theory and is uniquely suited for processing noisy, limited datasets. A key advantage of this technique is its ability to represent system trajectories in a compact form, making it computationally efficient. A representative test case is performed using a chaotic Lorenz system. Notably, this technique is capable of handling noise in data without yielding an unstable solution. A critical factor in this technique is selecting the most effective set of system trajectories, which is found to be a collection of random trajectories.

Naturalistic driving datasets are crucial for understanding real-world driving behaviors. However, existing datasets often fall short in depicting complex driving scenarios due to limited data. To address this issue, we compiled the SceneND dataset, which comprises 50 hours of video footage from 10 drivers. This research aims to showcase the value of the SceneND dataset in identifying various driving scenarios by employing scene analysis and recognition techniques. We then applied the dataset to train a scene recognition model, which achieved a top-5 accuracy of 80.5% when compared to the current state-of-the-art method. The SceneND dataset is available online for researchers to utilize.

In one-dimensional spatial dimensions, a newly introduced concept called reflected entropy has gained significance due to its ability to directly correspond with physical boundary conditions in higher dimensional spacetimes. This concept was found to be particularly useful in distinguishing between different phases of matter and in studying more complex scenarios involving boundaries and interfaces. Building upon this idea, we explore the reflected entropy within the context of boundary/conformal field theories and within the context of the boundary of a perfect fluid in a dual boundary conformal field theory described by the M/Ṁ boundary condition. We also extend our analysis to non-trivial boundary conditions and specifically examine a boundary condition representing a perfect fluid in a 3+1 dimensional spacetimes and how it affects the behavior of reflected entropy in one+1 dimensional spacetimes.

Recent research has explored the use of Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces (RIS) to improve wireless communication systems, but the performance of RIS is constrained by limitations such as hardware imperfections and interference caused by direct paths and surfaces. The complexity of accurately assessing these constraints is compounded by factors such as limited CP length, which hinders conventional CP-removal methods. A novel method is presented that employs a simplified CP-removed OFDM receiver and combines it with a gradient-enhanced Extreme Learning Machine (GE-ELM) to improve channel evaluation in RIS-assisted Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) systems. The proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in both low and high signal-to-noise ratios and exhibits exceptional resistance to adversarial attacks.

Nielsen and Chuang's book on quantum computation and coding has established a fundamental limit on single energy measurement accuracy. Recently, a new variation integral limit on energy measurement was proposed for single measurements. This new limit is not tied to a specific measurement strategy. We have found that an adaptive measurement strategy can achieve this not-tied limit, specifically for qubits. We have also noticed similarities between the standard and additive measurement limits, and between them and the not-tied single measurement limit. We have further extended these concepts to general measurements.

We are examining the deformation theory of G2-instantons on a nearly G2-manifold. Our research reveals that the linearized deformation operator of a G2-manifold's metric has a kernel comprised of G2-instanton A-harmonic forms. Furthermore, the full deformation theory of nearly G2-manifolds is based on the solution existence and uniqueness theorem we established for the nonlinear profile equation.

The COVID-19 pandemic has brought about an unprecedented need for effective control measures, which mobile contact tracing technology has helped to address.  This paper introduces a publicly available dataset, along with an analysis of the privacy risks associated with Android's proximity authentication feature used by National Contact Tracing (NCT) apps, which can potentially compromise user identity even with encryption.  In response, a library called PrivacyGuard has been developed to tackle this vulnerability, and an extensive dataset of device identifiers has been collected and shared, which can aid researchers and developers in assessing the security of NCT apps.  Furthermore, this research is the first of its kind to investigate proximity authentication vulnerabilities in NCT apps, and our findings have significant implications for app design and policy-making.  We anticipate that nct-apps will benefit from this work, and that other authors and reviewers can also utilize our shared knowledge and code to enhance the security of their projects.

Neural networks have long been the subject of intense study in biology, with their function still not fully understood. Researchers have used various theoretical models to shed light on neural signal processing, however the underlying mechanisms remain a mystery. A proposed theory suggests that neurons may employ quantum effects for signal computation, a concept we aim to explore and clarify in this study. By employing quantum information theory and using classical concepts to simulate quantum behavior, our research provides a practical approach for testing neural quantum hypotheses. A specific model involving spin systems and classical quantum simulations was developed to examine how neural signals could be processed. Results indicate that while some aspects of quantum computation may be applicable to neural systems, other concepts, such as spin chains and entanglement, may not be. Consequently, we believe that classically computing neural signals via 'quantum' decoders may provide the most effective approach for understanding neural signals and testing quantum behavior in neurons.

This text introduces the concept of a Shallow Embedding of C and its connection to Shallow Embedding of Formal Methods. Building on ACL2, a method for incorporating Shallow Embedding of C into ACL2 is presented to enable formal proofs written in ACL2. Furthermore, the discussion centers on translating verified properties expressed in ACL2 into proof-generating C code using the Racket translation tool. Two practical tools are described that implement this approach: C²A, a tool to translate C code into ACL2, and its complementary tool A²C, which translates ACL2 properties into C code. C²A is utilized to translate C code into formal proofs written in ACL2, while A²C is employed to generate verified C code from those same proofs. C²A is demonstrated using examples such as the Linux kernel's list manipulation functions, and A²C is employed using examples like the verification of binary search tree invariants.

Researchers have identified a possible asteroid family linked to Iochroma and further studied its members, particularly focusing on the distribution of family members in close proximity to Jupiter's 3:1 mean motion resonance. They found significant concentrations of both family and non-family asteroids near this resonance. Using Monte Carlo simulations, they modeled the long-term evolution of Iochroma family asteroids and discovered that the resurfacing of the primary asteroid, 39991 Iochroma, significantly impacts the family's dynamics at short timeframes. As a result, the final Iochroma family configuration exhibits multiple gaps, including those near the 3:1 Jupiter resonance and others such as those at 5:2 and 8:2 Saturnian resonances.

In this investigation, we establish a novel equation for Hurwitz Zeta functions, similar in nature to Rankin's equation, which we derive using double integral representations. By employing this equation, we examine specific cases, including single Zeta values and combinations with the Ramanujan Zeta function. We EBM-submit numerical computations supporting the validity of our findings.

We establish that for a logical circle group action on a complex vector space V, the elliptic cohomology of CP(V) with the same circle group action can be expressed as the completion of the ring Z[G] with a circle action, multiplied by the coefficient ring UE*([G/W]）。

We've developed a novel approach known as Machine Learning Algebraic Topology (MLAT), which integrates algebraic topological data analysis and machine learning methods. This synergy enables the creation of highly robust and adaptable machine learning models by leveraging the theoretical foundation provided by algebraic topology. The MLAT framework encompasses cutting-edge machine learning techniques, including deep learning, and addresses challenges in scientific research, particularly within particle physics, where topological data structures play a significant role. By combining machine learning and topological data analysis, we aim to provide comprehensive and interpretable models that are both theoretically sound and computationally efficient.

This research undertakes a comprehensive, to-the-next-leading-order analysis of the distribution patterns for $J/\psi$ produced in $e^{+}e^{-}$ collisions. This analysis compares two reactions: $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\eta_c$ and $e^{+}e^{-} \to J/\psi+\chi_{cJ}$, where the center-of-mass energy is approximately 10.6 GeV and the final state quarkium speeds are unspecified. This study revisits the QCD factorization theory for these reactions, focusing on the role of non-trivial distribution patterns within the $J/\psi$. The study identifies and evaluates various critical elements in the factorization theory, including the function describing the distribution patterns within $J/\psi$ and the properties of soft gluon exchanges. Furthermore, the study matches its findings with the properties of $J/\psi$ produced under leading-order QCD factorization. The findings demonstrate that next-to-leading-order corrections are substantial, with potential improvements in the study's accuracy.

Our research focuses on the misconceptions users have about their Signal PINs, which are intended to protect their accounts from unauthorized access in case of loss or theft. Through a combination of methods including an online survey, direct observation, and user recruitment, we discovered a significant number of Signal users, both casual and those with high engagement, mistakenly believe their PINs serve different purposes or have no purpose at all. This study is the first to examine the range of beliefs about the Signal PIN's function, highlighting the need for a user-friendly approach to communicate the purpose of the PIN and enhance its security role.

A comprehensive examination of solar power's precise energy savings and power capacity requirements is conducted for residential areas powered by rooftop solar panels, and this analysis is extended to commercial and industrial facilities as well, with a focus on all electric loads. A key mathematical technique, known as Gaussian quadrature, is employed to model the time-varying characteristics of solar power injection, and this method is used to calculate the net energy savings and specific power capacities needed to meet fixed electricity bills with a high degree of accuracy.

The curvature of the loss landscape plays a pivotal role in determining learning dynamics. The curvature is typically captured by the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM), but its massive computational requirements make it infeasible for deep learning. In this study, we delve into the relationship between FIM and the low-rank Gaussian Newton matrix. Our key finding is that by approximating the low-rank FIM, its essential characteristics are retained. Moreover, this approximation can be further condensed without compromising the representation of FIM's core data. Moreover, the curvature of a specific parameter is directly linked to its magnitude. Building upon this insight, we introduce a novel variational autoencoder (VAE) that learns a low-dimensional representation of the data space. The VAE is then used to estimate the low-rank FIM, resulting in an efficient approximation of the full FIM. Experimentally, our proposed method yields notable performance gains over existing techniques, with significantly reduced computational complexity.

This paper examines the impact of grammatical gender on representations of lexical items within multilingual language models. Leveraging a novel metric that quantifies the dependency of lexical representations on grammatical gender, we investigate the representation of distinct lexical categories in German, particularly focusing on gendered and non-gendered nouns. Our investigation encompasses gendered adjectives, which inherently carry gender information, as well as gender-triggering verbs, allowing us to deduce the implicit gender of the accompanying articles. Results reveal that, contrary to the handling of non-gendered nouns, gender-triggering verbs are often represented independently of their object's grammatical gender, likely due to the incorporation of the article's gender information in the verb's representation.

In the context of a rank-r algebraic group G, we determine how its stiffness for Siegel modular variety dimensions is limited by its highest rank, which we also see to be the largest possible value for a characteristic 0 stiffness. Furthermore, we discover that a characteristic p stiffness can at most be the rank of the group, which leads to a new upper limit on the maximum size of certain characteristics that preserve symmetry in to the weight of a characteristic p characteristic arithmetic stiffness. These findings build on previous research involving a knowledge base structure that is guided by a knowledge graph, specifically for characteristic 0 knowledge as first proposed by a particular framework.

Estimating an object's position is a crucial aspect of object recognition, which is a fundamental aspect of autonomous systems. This estimation enables a self-driving system to determine how objects are arranged in the environment, which in turn enables it to plan and execute its actions accordingly. However, most current approaches rely on having comprehensive datasets with annotated object bounding boxes for training. This dependency is costly and time-consuming. This research proposes a method for estimating object positions without the need for object-level bounding box annotations. This approach, which, like most modern methods, relies on image-level labels, and can be thought of as a form of "weak-to-zero-shot learning." The method, which, unlike object detection, does not require object bounding boxes, instead uses image-level labels to train the model, and can therefore, as the name suggests, estimate an object's position without the need for object-level training data. The method's "zero-shot capabilities" come from the use of category-level object features, which are in turn derived from image-level labels. The method's capabilities are demonstrated through the use of challenging datasets, and the results show that the method, which, unlike object detection, estimates an object's position without the need for object-level training data, and, as the name suggests, can therefore, as the name implies, estimate an object's position without the need for object-level training data. The method's capabilities are demonstrated through extensive experiments, and the results show that the method, which, as the name

Traffic forecasting is a crucial component for smart city applications, requiring the analysis of traffic patterns to enable effective decision-making. Traditional forecasting techniques, however, are limited by their reliance on vast datasets and the need for task-specific model training. This paper proposes a novel approach to large-scale traffic forecasting in data-sparse environments by automatically extracting key attributes based on traffic pattern similarities. A time series similarity method is used to identify and extract intrinsic characteristics, which are then applied to forecast traffic using a data-driven regression model. We demonstrate through extensive experiments using real traffic data that our technique significantly outperforms traditional methods, especially in data-sparse scenarios.

In the realm of causal inference, a fundamental problem involves inferring unobservable counterfactual facts based on cause-and-effect relationships found in a given graph, particularly when the underlying causal structure is unknown. A proposed solution called VACA utilizes a data-driven approach to infer a directed acyclic graph, then uses this structure to answer questions about unobservable scenarios. Specifically, this method can handle a range of queries, including simple "what if" scenarios where only one condition is specified, as well as complex scenarios where multiple conditions are specified. Additionally, VACA has been tested in both artificial and real-world datasets to assess its reliability and effectiveness.

The Irish LOFAR station benefits from an advanced real-time system called REALTA, designed to rapidly detect and respond to unpredictable celestial events. Built specifically for the Irish station, REALTA is now being used to study the fast-changing radio signals emitted by astrophysical transients, with initial results already revealing low-energy signals from gamma-ray bursts, including a detailed examination of the r-process site GW190814/GRB190814A. Furthermore, the system is set to support future research into fast change phenomena, such as those occurring in the Milky Way's FRBs and extragalactic blazars, enhancing our understanding of the universe's most dynamic processes.

Researchers have turned to machine learning and its associated algorithms to tackle complex physics problems, including those involving metaphotonics. Utilizing machine learning allows researchers to bypass traditional limitations and efficiently analyze vast amounts of data with minimal human intervention. Our work provides a comprehensive overview of machine learning and metaphotonics, shedding light on the interconnectedness of the two disciplines and illustrating how machine learning can bolster the development of metaphotonics in multiple ways.

As streaming services and home entertainment options grow in popularity, the value of movies is becoming less certain due to the unpredictable nature of home consumption. Researching factors that influence a movie's potential success is essential. We've created a comprehensive database containing information on nearly 12,000 movies released between 1913 and 2019. Utilizing regression analysis, we examined various attributes of these movies to identify the most significant factors that could impact revenue even before a movie is released. Our analysis revealed key takeaways for stakeholders in the movie industry, such as using an ensemble of predictive models to make informed decisions about assigning movies to different streaming and theatrical platforms.

In power systems, the intricate interplay between voltage stability and frequency stability is a critical aspect. Conventional frequency control methods, known as alternative frequency control (AFC), have been shown to contribute to frequency stability by providing enhanced speed and power. However, the current understanding of the impact of AFC on the underlying complex voltage dynamics is incomplete. In this study, we delve into the theoretical and practical implications of incorporating AFC in power grids, with a focus on the Poincar\'e-Sperner theorem. Our analysis reveals that the introduction of AFC can lead to the emergence of complex voltage dynamics, such as oscillations, in the power grid. Furthermore, the effectiveness of these oscillations varies depending on the specific network configuration, highlighting the need for careful evaluation of the impact of AFC on power grid performance.

Cyber-physical systems are becoming increasingly sophisticated, leading to a novel category of networks called cyber-physical networks (CPNs). The integration of cyber intelligence within CPNs is a promising approach to enhance the capabilities of individual CPS units and overall network performance. This work explores the integration of intelligent agents within CPNs, examining the benefits and challenges associated with introducing autonomy at the CPS unit and network levels. By integrating autonomous control within individual CPS units, we aim to enhance their resource management, fault tolerance, and energy efficiency. The application of autonomous agents at the network level can facilitate self-healing, self-organization, and efficient resource allocation. The report discusses various research areas, solution methodologies, and potential implementation methods, as well as the challenges and future research directions associated with embedding intelligence within CPNs.

Blazars are high-energy astrophysical sources that emit polarized light.
Using a new computational approach called MAPPIES, we simulate the polarization
patterns produced by various types of radiation interactions and account for the
complex geometry of the environment producing the light. Applying this method
to a large sample of 114 blazars, we find that many of these sources have
polarized light in the ultraviolet and soft X-ray ranges. Utilizing a simplified
model of geometric effects, we calculate that the electron population in these
sources consists of two distinct components: a high-energy power-law component
with a slope of 3.0 and a lower-energy Gaussian distribution with a peak at
around 100 keV. Our results suggest that the peak energy of the Gaussian
distribution around 100 keV is responsible for the peak polarized flux at
frequencies between 300 MHz and 30 THz. Furthermore, we find that the level of
polarization in X-rays is influenced by the slope of the power-law component.

We introduce a concept of effective field space and demonstrate its geometric structure, which anoints it with the properties of a complex manifold. This space possesses an anisotropic character, and we illustrate its connection to the de Sitter cone structure within the context of specific trigonometric complex landscapes. This relationship facilitates an analytic extension, which we apply to two specific models: the Higgs Inflation model and a large class of non-perturbative QFT landscapes. Notably, points located beyond the conformal bound are found to correspond to inflationary regimes in certain theories.

This research introduces a novel method for detecting identical-purity states in real-time. The protocol is suitable for implementing continuous measurements and relies on a stopping-criterion approach without premeditation, enabling adaptation to various states. The underlying threshold values are analytically determined and remain unaffected by various levels of noise or measurement noise. Simulated experiments indicate that the protocol can accurately detect coherent and attenuated light states with high efficiency. Furthermore, the protocol's capabilities are substantiated by findings and methods of statistical hypothesis testing theory.

Baryon formation via the process of some strings breaking apart and rearranging is a key aspect of the framework explaining how baryons are created from quark-gluon plasma. Baryons, composed of three cornerstones, can be understood as segments of QCD strings, twisted in a particular way. Baryon formation can be modeled by the interaction and entanglement of these twisted string parts, ultimately leading to the breaking apart of multiple strings and rearranging into baryonic structures. Specifically, the fragility of certain string configurations, particularly those with twists, is analyzed and found to decrease with increased complexity. Baryon formation through the entanglement and fragility of these strings is demonstrated and supported by simulations.

The observed Sun exhibits a north-south symmetry in travel time, which is typically attributed to the helioseismic time delay. To investigate this phenomenon, researchers conducted numerical magnetohydrodynamical simulations of active regions on quiet-Sun latitudes. These simulations revealed time-averaged mass flows, which, when measured, showed varying degrees of contribution to the helioseismic time delay. To assess this impact, researchers calculated the current-induced travel time delay. Their analysis showed that the mass flows' contribution to the helioseismic time delay was approximately 10-20 percent. Furthermore, researchers found that the current-induced time delay could account for a substantial portion, around 30-50 percent, of the observed quiet-Sun time delay. Their findings suggest a connection between the sun's time asymmetry and its mass flows.

In the realm of cosmology, primordial magnetic fields hold a place of significance. They are thought to have influenced the formation of the cosmos in a variety of ways and could potentially be observed in the cosmos today. Interestingly, recent studies have hinted at their possible imprint on the cosmos through binary compact objects, with the prospect of detection within the frequency range of LIGO and LISA. Given the limitations of these detectors, we investigated another area of the spectrum, specifically that of the Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) frequency range. Within this context, we utilized the Cosmic Magnetic Field Generator (CMFG) code to generate random magnetic field configurations and simulated the resulting gravitational wave (GW) signal. We then analyzed the power spectrum of GWs and found that the amplitude of GWs generated by different magnetic field configurations could be predicted by a scaling relation based on the magnetic field strength, the horizon scale, and the sound speed of the plasma. Furthermore, we found that the GW signal generated by primordial magnetic fields within the PTA frequency range could potentially be detected by the PTA network.

Light field data has the potential to be highly redundant, which has been the focus of the light field compression field for quite some time. Recent advances in deep learning techniques have significantly improved light field compression ratios, surpassing traditional methods by a significant margin. Despite this progress, compressed light field data still requires considerable time to decode, rendering it less effective in real-world applications. To address this issue, we introduce the first application of generative models in the light field compression field, specifically using encoder-decoder architectures. To leverage the properties of light field data and minimize redundancy, we develop a novel parallax-aware view synthesis approach, utilizing 4 adjacent angle maps as input, and further enhance it with residual learning and a loss function tailored for peak signal-to-signal noise ratio in the visible spectrum, incorporating human visual sensitivity. To facilitate real-time decoding, we analyze the properties of the residual network and leverage these findings in our design. Our deep compression approach is evaluated on a publicly available light field dataset and outperforms existing methods in terms of redundancy reduction, particularly at high compression ratios, while also achieving real-time decoding speeds.

For many low-resource languages, interactive models like cross-lingual info retrieval with multi-modal interaction significantly improve search performance over traditional methods. However, these models' inability to scale effectively to large datasets poses a significant limitation. In this case study, it's demonstrated that combining both interactive and non-interactive approaches yields unique insights and potentially enhances irMAP performance for a set of languages. By analyzing the contributions of various components to the final search performance, it's found that leveraging multiple modalities can lead to better search outcomes, especially in visual-based ir tasks. Furthermore, it's shown that using non-interactive models can effectively contribute to ir performance and is thus recommended as a practical and efficient approach for multi-modal tasks.

This study aimed to identify the most suitable techniques for generating small area estimates in low- and middle-income countries. Our analysis involved developing four different models to simulate data on cigarette consumption, along with three design-based models. By utilizing Stata and R, we compared statistical and computational methods in terms of prediction accuracy, as well as assessed software feasibility for countries with limited resources. Results showed that the estimated design-based models outperformed one-way ANOVA and the empirical Bayesian small area estimation model, but the latter was the most accurate for all scenarios. It is suggested that statistical and computational methods can effectively support policy-making in low- and middle-income countries, though design-based models proved to be more accessible for countries with limited software capabilities.

The Kelly criterion, a well-established strategy for gambling, has been successfully applied in the realm of financial trading. Although it has been long recognized in the scientific community as potentially quantum-enhanceable, previous research focused solely on discrete variable systems. In this study, we introduce a novel method for variable-based gambling using a coherent state, thereby enabling the first quantum profit via the variable aspect. Furthermore, this experimentally feasible concept can be set up with existing quantum technology and may pave the way for real-world quantum-variable-based gambling applications.

This study is a comprehensive theoretical examination of the electronic characteristics of the recently synthesized two-dimensional materials, including MoSi$_2$N$_4$, WSi$_2$N$_4$, WP$_2$Ge$_2$N$_4$, and MSi$_2$P$_2$N$_4$. We have identified a distinct stacking arrangement in MSi$_2$N$_4$ and MSi$_2$P$_2$N$_4$ that is different from the commonly observed structure of other maateerates. We have also found that MSi$_2$N$_4$ and MSi$_2$P$_2$N$_4$ exhibit similar quasiparticle band arrangements, with an unusual formation where the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) bands cross, unlike other maateerates. We have confirmed that MSi$_2$N$_4$ and MSi$_2$P$_2$Ge$_2$N$_4$ exhibit excitonic behavior at room temperature.

The following decay has been studied using proton collision data with an integrated luminosity of 9$^{+}$fb collected by the LHCb experiment: $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$. An excess signal has been observed above the background noise with a statistical significance exceeding 5 sigma. After correcting for various factors, the absolute branching fraction for this process is estimated to be $(1.19 \pm 0.18) \times 10^{-6}$. Furthermore, this process has a flavour-unchanged branching fraction ratio of $(1.22 \pm 0.13) \times 10^{-4}$ with respect to a well-known process $\Lambda_b^0 \to p \bar{p} \Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$. These results are presented for comparison with theoretical models in flavour physics.

A preliminary analysis of the ALMA observations of TW HMM-1, a Class 0 protostar, reveals a preliminary model of the protoplanetary disk's evolution. Using simulations, we investigated how a disk forms from the collapse of a spherical core. To do this, we modeled the core as a uniform sphere with an isothermal structure and added an exponential density enhancement. We ran high-resolution simulations using a three-dimensional hydrodynamic code that incorporated magnetic effects and considered the effects of molecular cooling. We found that a disk forms in the simulation and its size correlates with the mass of the core and molecular cooling efficiency. We also determined that a dynamic viscosity model is necessary to match the observed disk sizes. We also found evidence of core fragmentation in our simulations, which suggests that the observed fragments are unlikely to be the result of gravitational instability. We propose that TW HMM-1, a class 0 protostar, formed from a prestellar core with a mass of approximately 0.03 solar masses.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes are hindered by the complex effects of the Earth's atmosphere, which vary depending on the object being observed. By observing celestial bodies through the same atmospheric column, these distortions can be partially neutralized. However, the differing requirements for correcting blue and red light pose a challenge. To address this, a new atmospheric distortion model has been developed, utilizing a customized camera to directly measure the shape of stellar images. This model relies on two key parameters to represent the atmosphere's distortions, which were tested on various star colors and showed promising results. Furthermore, the model was also used alongside other methods to correct stellar images, demonstrating its potential to enhance the quality of astronomical observations.

This study introduces a novel approach to sparse multi-period time series regression with a focus on high-dimensional data. Building on the Bayesian linear regression model, a hierarchical Bayesian model is developed to induce sparsity. The integration of the Garch model allows for time series error analysis, while the Bayesian framework provides a natural way to model uncertainty. The proposed model incorporates two key sparsity-inducing mechanisms: a Gamma prior on regression coefficients and a Beta distribution on variable inclusion probabilities, which can be inferred using Bayesian variational inference. The method demonstrates superior performance in handling noisy and high-dimensional data compared to the maximum likelihood estimation.

This note demonstrates that a topological group $G$ serves as the logic of a constant first-order theory $T$ if and only if $G$ possesses the property of being compact and Hausdorff. As a subsidiary finding, we establish that the Bohr compactification of a Pontryagin dual group $\mathbf{X}$ applies to the Stone space of its associated Stone dual group $\mathbf{X}^\vee$.

Federated learning, a decentralized FL approach, prioritizes user privacy through local data retention and encrypted communication. Nevertheless, it encounters difficulties in addressing the potential for bias against specific user groups or data. This study investigates the FL framework in relation to two critical fairness methods, namely, group fairness (independent of data) and individual fairness, and highlights the inherent trade-offs within the FL framework, also taking privacy into account. The findings reveal strict limitations that apply to both forms of fairness in FL, and essentially demonstrate the impossibility of an FL algorithm to achieve these fairness standards without compromising on accuracy. Moreover, considering privacy as a factor, our results establish tight theorems that quantify the trade-offs between FL's accuracy and the implementation of fairness and privacy within the framework. The individual fairness criteria pose the most significant challenge, and in order to address this, we introduce a strategy for bias-reduced FL, utilizing external 'fairness reference groups' to establish fair performance across diverse data sets. The proposed method demonstrates the feasibility of an FL algorithm to achieve notable levels of individual fairness, and provides practical evidence of the technique's potential to mitigate bias in real-world applications.

A theoretical model is suggested that combines the dark matter and dark energy phenomena by leveraging the U(1)_X extension of the Standard Model with a superposition of both RH neutrino and singlet fermion dark matter. A theoretical link is established between the dark matter mass and the dark energy scale through the spontaneous breaking of electroweak symmetry, with a Right-handed Neutrino serving as a bridge between the two sectors. A Right-handed Neutrino also functions as a mediator of U(1)_X forces, with its mixing with the Standard Model neutrino providing the primary decay pathway for the Z' boson. The U(1)_X gauge coupling remains extremely weak due to the high scale of Z' boson decays, making it nearly indistinguishable from minimal dark energy.

We have developed an innovative approach to maximize the wireless powered network's throughput, which involves devices that can transfer data and a reflective IRS to enhance short-distance communication. Since joint optimization of devices' transmission rates, power, and IRS placements is a complex problem, we've made two significant simplifications: 1) we've held power levels constant and focused on optimizing device transmission patterns using a deep learning model, which bypasses the complex power calculation; 2) we've focused only on reflecting the IRS's phases, not its placement, as well as the devices that transmit data, making the problem more manageable. The result is a new deep learning approach that utilizes real-world channel information, including interference and noise, to optimize phases through phase mapping layers, which simplifies the problem and improves efficiency. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated by comprehensive numerical results, showing a substantial 10-fold increase in throughput compared to a baseline system without interference.

For the first time, researchers used both $\gamma$-ray detection and magnetic multipole orientations to map the energy levels of the $^{186}$Hg nucleus with a focus on its properties. This investigation focused on the energy levels of $^{186}$Hg in the spin range of 40 to 56$\hbar$, providing a more accurate examination of its nuclear characteristics than previous studies. The study's results were then compared with predictions from three different theoretical models, revealing discrepancies between the actual and predicted energy levels. This analysis was further supported by a detailed review of the results from a 2014 study involving the $\gamma$-ray spectrum of $^{186}$Hg.

A unified framework is established that combines the generation of matter imbalance in the universe and the existence of dark matter within a single structure. This model is based on a specific arrangement of fermion fields and involves the complex relationships between these fields in a way that influences both the dark matter density in the universe and the matter-antimatter imbalance during a specific period of time. As a result, the model exhibits an intricate connection between dark matter and the concept of matter-antimatter asymmetry, leading to a specific relationship between these concepts that can be used to constrain various aspects of the model's parameters. This relationship is particularly significant for understanding the dark matter density in the universe.

This paper introduces a novel approach to designing data-driven controllers that can achieve multiple complex tasks simultaneously, such as reaching a target, locomotion and taking off, without the need for side information about the system's dynamics. The proposed controller accomplishes this by leveraging a task-specific function that guides the system towards its goals, while a task-general function adapts to differences in the system model, using only scarce side information. The novel side information can be obtained by recording a single, imperfect trajectory, enabling the development of controllers for applications where side information is hard to obtain, such as biological and soft systems. The approach has been tested on a 10-degree-of-freedom soft robotic fish in a complex, three-dimensional environment and has shown promising results, outperforming a state-of-the-art controller that relies on side information and a state-of-the-art controller with a similar architecture but no task generalization capabilities, demonstrating up to 20x energy savings over the no-task generalization controller and 2.5x over the task-specific controller that relies on system dynamics.

We found 24 correlation functions that connect key elements within the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory, providing an extension of the ward relationships in this context, which connect principles of conformal invariance and gauge symmetry within the theory. We then used these relationships to derive novel identities that connect various correlation functions, which we verified through our computational methods, offering a more comprehensive understanding of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ conformal field theory.

Action recognition in partial sequences of actions relies heavily on how different actions relate to one another, especially in sequences that overlap or are out of order. Current research has made progress in this area, but most methods struggle when dealing with complex action relationships, especially those that involve multiple actions. To address this limitation, we have developed a new approach called Relation GAN, which uses action relationships to improve recognition accuracy. Relation GAN generates action representations and uses them to identify the most likely action sequence. By focusing on the relationships between actions, our method is able to accurately predict actions even in complex videos with multiple people and overlapping actions. Relation GAN has been tested on three datasets, including NTU-RGB+D 50 (split46), HMDB-51, and Kinetics 600, and our results show significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods.

A recently introduced method for quantum key exchange called twin-field QKD has achieved a breakthrough in overcoming the fundamental limit on secure key generation rates, previously thought to be restricted by the square root of the transmission loss. Unlike traditional methods, TFD allows for the secure generation of keys over long distances by attributing key generation to interference patterns at the receiver's end, rather than source emissions. While reducing costs and enhancing robustness to various implementation flaws, a major limitation of TFD is its reliance on precise phase locking between the sender and receiver. To overcome this, we propose a variation of TFD in this work, overcoming the need for phase locking, thereby simplifying system design and enhancing security. Our approach relies on establishing a shared reference phase between the sender and receiver using classical communication, rather than maintaining a phase-locked connection. Our feasibility analysis indicates that the revised protocol shares many similarities with conventional TFD in terms of key generation rates and security levels.

Let H be a Hilbert space and T be the algebra of bounded operators on H, with S being a subalgebra consisting of compact operators. A subsymmetric sequence of operators in T is defined, and its associated maximal abelian subalgebra is denoted as A. Under the assumption that H is separable, it is proven that every operator in A can be represented as the sum of an operator in S and a unitary operator. For specific choices of H, including the Hardy and Bergman spaces, operators in A can be explicitly described. In particular, when H is the Hardy space, it is shown that every operator in A corresponds to a Toeplitz operator. In addition, it is proven that the weak closure of A equals T. A study of operators in A that commute with shift operators is also conducted and related algebraic structures are explored. Furthermore, it is shown that certain subalgebras of A are isomorphic to Toeplitz algebras and possess a specific dimension. In a separate finding, it is proven that every operator in A corresponds to a Toeplitz operator when H is replaced with the Bergman space, and it is also demonstrated that this result fails for certain weighted Bergman spaces.

Object detection using description text has been explored in the past, but existing approaches have significant limitations such as relying on a small number of description types or using inefficient detection methods. To address these issues, a new method called Pseudo-BBox has been proposed. This method involves using visual features to locate objects and descriptions to identify them, effectively combining the benefits of both visual and textual information. To efficiently train this model, data augmentation has been employed to create diverse pseudo labels from description-text pairs. This method has been shown to achieve state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks and outperforms existing methods that use description-text pairs without additional training.

A region surrounding the S1 shock in Rho Ophiuchus A is analyzed using SOFIA and Hubble data, examining A, B and C clumps at various distances from the shock.
