The primary goal of sequential recommender systems is to suggest the most suitable item to a user based on their item sequences. However, these sequences often contain users performing multiple tasks simultaneously, which, if not addressed, can degrade the performance of these recommender systems. To tackle this issue, we introduce a novel approach called Latent User Purpose Modeling (LUPM) to accurately capture and analyze the users' underlying objectives. By leveraging LUPM, we can identify and isolate the items contributing to the users' primary task, thereby providing more precise recommendations. Furthermore, we evaluate the effectiveness of LUPM using real-world datasets and compare it to established sequential recommender systems, yielding satisfactory results.

It's crucial in numerical applications to express the double confluent Heun equation in reducible form, allowing for connection to other special functions and facilitating the matching of asymptotic numerical series solutions. Furthermore, we have discovered an extensive and systematic method to unfold the source term of this equation, which was previously thought to be irreducible. Remarkably, this unfolded equation exhibits rich monodromy properties and a complete set of quadratures. We also demonstrate how both the unfolded and reduced equations can be transformed into the Fabry normal form and establish a correspondence with the generalized Lamé equation.

We investigate the low-rank matrix estimation problem in situations where the matrix entries follow independent but not uniform statistical distributions. The product of two matrix entries has a mean that corresponds to the product of their individual expected values, and their variances are determined by separate functions applied to the absolute squared values of their individual expected values, which may differ across entries. This differing statistical property is referred to as groupwise heteroskedasticity. Many real-world scenarios, including analyzing cell-to-cell differences in biological experiments and understanding differences in light intensity in astronomical observations, can be viewed as low-rank matrix estimation problems with groupwise heteroskedasticity. We show that when considering the widely used maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) and its computationally simpler counterpart, the method of moments (MOM), the estimator's error for each entry is largely determined by the degree of heteroskedasticity for that specific entry. Furthermore, we prove that no estimator, including the optimal one, can achieve an error smaller than the sum of the MLE and the square root of the degree of heteroskedasticity for that specific entry. These results are supported through the development of theoretical arguments as well as simulation experiments.

We establish an inherent topological model of the band theory, disregarding symmetry constraints. In a general case, topological models are often based on crystalline symmetry and reduced models with high symmetry encode higher-order topological phenomena. By removing symmetry requirements, any gapped model can be described by a continuous map from the parameter space to the space of unitary matrices. This geometric structure can be decomposed into simpler components, the simplest of which are the band theories with a single band, and more complex models are those that can only exist due to a non-trivial homotopy class. In a space with no holes, all band theories are trivial and can be continuously deformed into a gapless model, and this proof relies on fundamental concepts such as the homotopy group and the concept of a path.

The ratio of semi-inclusive $\epsilon$ Lepton Flavour Invariance (LFI) ratios in
$ b \to s \ell^+ \ell^- $ transitions is studied as a novel, hadron-weak phase
insensitive observable that is potentially sensitive to new physics. We find
that this ratio is not influenced by non-local QCD effects and is well described
by the standard operator product expansion approach. Our fit to this observable
yields a value of $ R_{\epsilon,2}^{CP} = 0.99^{+0.15}_{-0.16} $ and
$ R_{\epsilon,1}^{CP} = 0.97^{+0.12}_{-0.13} $, which is consistent with
lepton flavour universality and the standard model. We also provide a method for
including $ 1/m_b^2 $ power corrections in theoretical predictions.

This study presents a novel approach to designing a decentralized finite impulse response filter set that achieves independent objectives in each of an integrated network of interconnected systems. We develop a stochastic finite impulse response filter set that minimizes the desired error at a central node while ensuring the invertibility of the collective system. To improve adaptability, the proposed method can be easily integrated into a Markov decision process framework, allowing the central controller to optimize its parameters in real-time based on dynamic channel conditions. This method can be seamlessly combined with existing adaptive control strategies to improve overall performance. Our approach is evaluated through a series of simulations, demonstrating its practical application and effectiveness.

The COVID19 pandemic has caused significant disruption globally, with the second stage bringing about widespread loss and hardship. One of the most effective ways to combat the virus is by identifying and isolating those infected as quickly as possible. To alleviate the burden on healthcare workers, researchers have turned to advanced technology, specifically deep learning, to aid in diagnosing COVID19 via chest X-ray imaging. A novel two-stage classification system is proposed, employing BERT for both visual and audio inputs to diagnose COVID19. This approach involves incorporating a Wav2Vec model trained on COVID19 patient coughs, alongside the development of a customized dataset for enhanced diagnostic capabilities.

This article offers a concise overview of fundamental graph theory concepts, tailored to assist network scientists in tackling intricate scientific challenges. It meticulously defines core graph notions, explores essential theorems, and delves into cutting-edge research areas, such as graph representations learned by machine, their visualizations, and the analysis of massive graphs through dimension reduction. Although primarily focused on unweighted, undirected graphs, some sections acknowledge nuances, like directed graphs, weighted graphs, and asymmetric properties. The article serves as a navigational aid for graph theory resources, including software tools and further reading materials.

The study of eco-evolutionary dynamics is a complex process influenced by the rates and drivers of ecological and evolutionary interactions. These interactions can be classified into deep-seated, gradual processes and more recent, rapid cycles. We develop a unified mathematical framework to analyze and compare these different timescales and their impact on eco-evolutionary systems. By employing a combination of dimensionless variables and a generalized ODE system, our model allows for a quantitative assessment of the relative influence of timescales on the behavior and outcomes of eco-evolutionary systems. We apply this model to three fundamental ecological models: the Lotka-Volterra model, competition and evolutionary branching and the Allee effect and stabilization by evolution, to demonstrate the effectiveness of our model. We find that ecological and evolutionary timescales play a significant role in determining eco-evolutionary outcomes and that our model provides a valuable tool for assessing the impact of timescales on the stability and behavior of eco-evolutionary systems.

Building speech AI systems that cannot be tricked is becoming more and more important.
So far, research into adversarial attacks on speech models has been limited to simple synthetic examples.
To improve this situation, we created a larger and more realistic test set featuring thousands of advanced adversarial samples.
Using state-of-the-teacher methods, we examined how well speech self-supervised learning (SSL) can detect these simpler adversative examples, and we compared it to traditional speech parameterization.
We found that SSL is less susceptible to these complex adversarial tests, highlighting the need for further testing on even more sophisticated speech adversarial data, and building better evaluation tools.

This study draws upon blockchain exchange data to examine whether adoption patterns of decentralized peer-to-peer digital currency exchanges are adaptive in response to changes in network size, transaction volumes, and time. Specifically, this study examines exchanges such as XMR, CLOAKCOIN, MONERO, and FLUX for potential self-similarity in their growth patterns. The findings confirm that the exchange growth patterns are not only adaptive but also follow a specific long-term power-law distribution. Notably, the correction critical exponent shows a strong negative correlation with the network size, transaction frequency, and time intervals for a specific range, implying that exchanges become more sensitive to fluctuations as the network size increases.

Bounded random variables, in any dataset, can lead to a massive number of possible realizations, making probability distributions essential for practical analysis. However, the lack of information about a variable's lower bound can hinder statistical analysis. This becomes particularly problematic when analyzing the "last observation carried forward" approach in longitudinal data, which often results in missing values. This study presents an innovative method using the E-value to conduct a sensitivity analysis for missing data within a non-informative context. This method generates a posterior distribution for the unknown lower bound of the variable in question. Subsequently, various statistical estimates are calculated based on this posterior distribution, providing a built-in mechanism for uncertainty quantification. Through comprehensive simulation experiments and an actual case study, the proposed methodology is thoroughly evaluated and tested.

We finish the list of symmetry extensions for the quantum torus $\mathcal{Z}_\theta$ by applying a specific algebra $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$. Previous extensions have been identified in [BMS20]. Our work on the algebra's central element is what enables the extensions. Using a specific element $Z$, we can create a homomorphism from $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2) \to U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)^\mathbf{t}$, where $\mathbf{t}$ denotes the $\mathbb{Z}$-grading. This allows the creation of a $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)^\mathbf{t}$-module structure on $\mathcal{Z}_\theta$. The resulting action is then used to construct a quotient quotient, known as the quantum surface $Z_\theta$, based on the algebra's trace invariant. This action lifts to a corresponding graded tensor product structure on $\mathcal{Z}_\theta\otimes_\mathbb{C} U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)^\mathbf{t}$. By applying a specific method involving a $\mathbb{Z}$-grading, we can construct Hilbert C*-algebras from these structures and obtain KMS states for the corresponding C*-algebras. These correspond to a family of free quasi-free states on the quantum surface

The convergence of next-generation Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) and blockchain technology has paved the way for novel applications in vehicular networks. IoVs is expected to see widespread adoption of autonomous vehicles, while blockchain technology offers secure, transparent, and tamper-resistant data management. Their synergy has sparked interest in blockchain-empowered federated learning (FL) frameworks for IoVs. This study aims to explore and compare various FL frameworks empowered by blockchain technology in IoVs. A comprehensive systematic literature review was conducted, evaluating over 100 research studies. After filtering, 26 studies were selected, revealing four primary application scenarios: resource allocation, training model, data privacy protection, and incentive mechanisms. This study categorizes existing FL frameworks based on blockchain functionality and FL architecture, highlighting four architecture types: edge cloud, vehicle cluster, road side unit, and road side server. Furthermore, FL frameworks are classified into four types: client-server, peer-to-peer, hierarchical, and hybrid, based on network topology and communication patterns.

Alfred Wegener Universität, Bremen, Germany

Jets originating from heavy flavor production are analyzed at 5.02 TeV for both fully reconstructed D mesons (including D0, D+, and S0) and their corresponding semileptonic decay products (including D0*, D+, and S0), utilizing the ALICE experiment's data. The transverse momentum distributions of these mesons are calculated within the central rapidity range (|y| < 0.8) and are compared against theoretical models incorporating NNPDF3.1 nuclear PDFs. Additionally, the total cross sections of the mesons are estimated, with the results for D mesons (including D0, D+, and S0) being 30.0 millibarns, with an error margin of 0.9 millibarns, and the results for charm production (including D0, D+, and J/S) being estimated at 2.21 millibarns, with an error margin of 0.04 millibarns. The estimated results are compared against theoretical models incorporating NNPDF3.1 nuclear PDFs.

A large-scale dilution refrigerator with four branches and 1,000 millikelvin warming levels at the Fermilab Computing Science Division demonstrates the capability to support multiple superconducting quantum processing units, enabling up to 100 million qubits. This report provides a detailed description of the refrigerator's design, including its specific components, such as vacuum pumps, compressors, and stage temperatures. It also showcases three of the four operational stages, which house various electronic components, such as amplifiers, multiplexers, and board-level control systems. Furthermore, the report discusses the quantum processing unit's cryogenic and control systems, which include optimized printed circuit boards, high-performance CPUs, and highly sensitive electronic measurement equipment.

This study examines common exploitation techniques targeting cryptographic vulnerabilities within Python applications, revealing an alarming prevalence of critical flaws like weak encryption algorithms and flawed authentication methods. By integrating tools such as BruteForce, CTFtools, and Jumbo, attackers can efficiently launch brute force and dictionary-based attacks, often with limited success. The research also highlights a lack of emphasis on this area in the Python community, suggesting that current cryptography resources are outdated and overly technical. The findings provide valuable insights into the most effective and common crypto abuse methods, with implications for future research and community guidance.

This paper introduces an efficient and scalable method for tag-based object detection in urban environments. Given the substantial cost of developing diverse tag datasets for numerous objects, our approach leverages a limited dataset and diverse human tagging to produce a reliable detector for a specific tag. The main challenge of integrating diverse tagging from multiple users into a coherent tag that minimizes detection errors is addressed through our novel framework, the Voting and Aggregating Labeling Engine. Our experiments confirm the effectiveness of this method in producing accurate results on real-world datasets.

Seismic reflectivity inversion using deep learning offers a promising solution to address the limitations of traditional inversion methods. While most current techniques rely on uniformly sparse or non-sparse deep learning methods, they are unsuitable for applications where the seismic reflectivity is nonuniformly sparse. This study proposes a novel Proximal Average Network (SPAN), a deep learning method tailored for applications with nonuniform sparse seismic reflectivity. Additionally, a framework based on nonuniform sparse seismic reflectivity with a convex optimization approach is introduced to address computational challenges. Unlike conventional optimization methods, SPAN is capable of handling nonuniform sparse seismic reflectivity. Numerical results demonstrate that SPAN outperforms other methods, including k-SNR, L1-norm, L0-norm, Lp-norm, Lp-norm+L0-norm, and Lp-norm+L1-norm optimization methods, while being comparable to Deepk-SNR. Furthermore, a comprehensive numerical analysis examines how the seismic reflectivity, noise, and Lp-norm affect the performance of SPAN.

This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-like spaces, specifically on BMOA, plus the space X^+ and X^-. We establish relationships between the infinitesimal generator of a semigroup $\{\mathcal{T}_t\}_{t\geq 0}$ in the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$, and the uniform boundedness in BMOA of the semigroup, as well as identifying quasicontinuity sets $Q$ for $\mathcal{T}'_t$. Additionally, we explore the operator $V_{\mathcal{T}_t,\phi}$ on BMOA, defined by $(V_{\mathcal{T}_t,\phi}f)(z)=\mathcal{T}_tf(z)\phi(z)$, and determine its compactness and Hilbert-Schmidt properties.

We introduce a technique for computing the fusion coefficients of a three-dimensional topological quantum field model using the finite-size haagerup unitary modular tensor model. Our proposed method, applicable to any model, relies on the fact that Haagerup's $S$-matrix elements can be expressed as sums of complex numbers with a common magnitude of 1/4!. By initiating calculations with small systems, we can determine all possible haagerup tensor category fusion coefficients, along with their corresponding complex values, through a reorganization of a large-system expansion in inverse powers of $L$. This technique enables us to recover even $4N$-system expansion coefficients from smaller systems with specific scaling. Applying this method to all non-trivial haagerup fusion rules, we derive universal scaling corrections to bulk haagerup model cylinder wavefunction coefficients in terms of central charge, genus, scaling dimension, and conformal dimension. Our results align with a recent study on universal corrections to large-geometry $q$-deformed minimal model fusion coefficients, and demonstrate that universal corrections are determined by a Haagerup $S$-matrix element commonality.

In recent years, deep learning models have largely dominated the field of part-of-speech tagging, but historical corpora pose significant challenges for these models due to diverse and unpredictable tag sets. As a result, research has primarily focused on tag-bias transfer learning, but this approach can lead to the propagation of historical biases, such as an overabundance of common tags derived from modern corpora. This paper proposes setting the tag bias aside and instead develops a novel method for predicting the POsT sets that historical texts belong to, thereby eliminating tag-bias issues. The experimental evaluation of our approach on 18 German dialect corpora from the 18th to the 21st centuries demonstrates the effectiveness of our method in accurately identifying the POsT sets of historical texts, even with limited knowledge of the tag sets.

This research focuses on a class of highly irregular functions, specifically one where a function, f, is integrable if it is bounded, measurable, and for any set, E, with a zero measure, the set where function, f, is also zero measure, the integral of function, f times function, g is equal to the integral of function, f times function, g for all function, g, that are continuous and bounded. Notable improvements over traditional integrability theories include the fact that function, f is Riemann-integrable if and only if it is also function, f-integrable, and similarly for Lebesgue-integrability with function, f being measurable and bounded. Moreover, an inequality exists between function, f-integration and Riemann integration and Lebesgue integration. An interesting inequality involving the function, f-integration exists that can be used to solve the Young integral and handle discontinuous functions with discontinuities of a measure. Additionally, a representation theorem exists for function, f-integration that can be used to solve the representation of function, f-integration when function, f is function, f-integrable and bounded and measurable, with measure, μ, extended to a function, f-integration when function, f is extended to a function, f-integrable and bounded and measurable, with measure, μ.

This study aims to address a pivotal aspect of formal methods - developing formal models based on cities' expressed needs - by employing an innovative assistant that streamlines formal specification. Current formal methods tools necessiate users to input and type requirements into a unified language, a task that can be laborious and error-prone. In an effort to alleviate this burden, we have devised an intelligent assistant that leverages natural language processing to automatically convert cities' verbal requirements into formal logical expressions.

This paper introduces a novel approach to mitigate quantum errors, inspired by the concept of backtracking in path optimization. Building on this, we develop the Hidden Inverses Protocol (HIP), which enables reversible quantum computation. Specifically, HIP is tailored for surface codes, a prevalent quantum error correction method, and is specifically adapted for implementation on superconducting circuits. On these devices, universal quantum computation is achieved through a combination of single-qubit gates and the logical operations of logical CNOT, X, and Z gates, designed to efficiently correct surface code errors. Simulations indicate that HIP outperforms traditional decoding methods in efficiently correcting error bursts. Furthermore, HIP's underlying principles are theoretically sound and hold potential for broader applications in other quantum correction methods and hidden inverse-based algorithms.

Equivalence relations can be represented as binary relations on a given category.
To expand on this, we propose replacing equivalence relations with preorder relations,
but this requires modifying the property of being fully cocartesian to its reflective counterpart,
which we define as weakly cocartesian. Unlike the original property, the new property is specifically
cocartesian in categories that are well-pointed. Furthermore, we establish that any preorder
can be represented in any regular category that has pullbacks, subject to the condition that it is
reflective.

The application of multivariate spatial models is explored for analyzing multiple extreme environments at specific locations within the British Isles. By incorporating a parameter-sharing multivariate Gumbel copula model and an extreme value regression model, an efficient Bayesian framework can be developed. This approach allows for the estimation of extreme environment conditions and associated return periods. Additionally, simulation-based prediction intervals can be obtained for an extreme environment at a location. Results from a case study in the British Isles show that a 100-year return period at certain locations can be predicted for concurrent extreme wave height and temperature, which can be observed between 7:00 and 11:00 British Summer Time.

Multimodal models that combine visual and textual inputs have shown significant promise in handling various computer vision tasks, yet they often face challenges from text noise, such as typos, which can hinder model learning. Current approaches typically rely on a one-size-fits-all strategy, lacking the ability to differentiate between the impact of specific types of text noise. VT-CLIP, a new framework introduced in this work, addresses this limitation by incorporating two key components: a similarity-based filtering mechanism that identifies and removes text noise similar to visual features, and a text regeneration module that creates synthetic data to reinforce the correlation between visual features and their corresponding text. Through the integration of these components, VT-CLIP effectively improves the performance of CLIP on complex computer vision tasks, including inference and image retrieval.

This research focuses on developing an efficient method for handling noisy systems of matrices, where each matrix represents a quantum operator acting on a high-dimensional space. We define 'transitioning an operator' as a strategy, utilized by a player in an advanced game of operators, for countering an adversary providing adversarial noisy matrices. Unlike prior work, which concentrated on individual noisy matrices or specific matrix entries, our approach considers the dynamic nature of matrices in response to the player's choices, introducing a general framework for operator transitioning in complex matrix systems. We introduce two new techniques for transitioning operators: (1) a reduction algorithm efficiently translating adversarial matrix systems into highly connected graph systems and (2) a novel graph-based transitioning approach leveraging recent findings on noisy traceless matrix games and quantum walk. We also present two types of operator transitioning methods for noisy systems, including deterministic and randomized approaches, along with a comprehensive analysis of their strengths and limitations, including trade-offs for noisy quantum systems in high-dimensional spaces.

We identify the section functors of specific quaternionic K-theory spectral sequences, which link to Eilenberg-Mac Lane spectra defined over quaternionic rings with the property $-1 = +1$. Our spectral data is derived from prior work by Bognar-Rudolph.

Given a two-dimensional F-roaring local ring R, we calculate the exact F-slope sequence for its canonical module, denoted as $\omega_R$, and we prove that if the F-slope sequence of $\omega_R$ coincides with its Hilbert slope sequence, then R satisfies the property of being F-regular.

Advanced medical imaging technologies are rapidly evolving, with deep learning techniques achieving notable performance in image interpretation tasks such as disease identification, but significant challenges remain in achieving consistent performance on new datasets. In order to facilitate the development of medical imaging applications, data sharing and model comparison are becoming increasingly crucial. In light of this need, we developed Highdicom, a Python library that leverages DICOM and high-dimensional image data to produce high-quality datasets and model predictions in the medical field. Through both simulated and real-world examples, we demonstrate Highdicom's ability to efficiently generate large volumes of labeled data and uncertainty-based predictions in a fast and memory-efficient manner. Additionally, we compare Highdicom's level of DICOM compliance to that of alternative methods and find it to be superior. Highdicom's versatility is further showcased through its ability to support popular deep learning models and various post-processing and analysis techniques for image data.

In this study, the Holtzmann-Roman (Kodama) Noether current associated with diffeomorphisms is investigated for its contribution from the Gibbons-York-Hawking boundary term in the Einstein-Hilbert action. The resulting current, $J^{\mu}_{	ext{KH}}$, encompasses a key component, $\kappa_{	ext{KH}}G^{\mu
u}_{	ext{GH}}n_
u+\mathcal{I}_{	ext{KH}}^\mu$, where the boundary term involving the metric varies smoothly across the null boundary, with $\kappa_{	ext{KH}}$ representing the surface gravity and $n_
u$ being the unit normal vector to the boundary. By applying a vector field $\xi^\mu$, which generates the Virasoro algebra on the null boundary, the zero mode component of $\xi^\mu$, denoted as $f(r)$, enables a decomposition of $J^{\mu}_{	ext{KH}}_	ext{AH}$ into a Killing horizon and asymptotic symmetry component. Consequently, the null boundary's entropy corresponding to $\xi^\mu$, denoted as $S_	ext{KH}$, is derived from the boundary term involving the metric.

In the study of genomics, identifying meaningful features from raw DNA sequence data is a critical challenge. To address this problem, we have developed an unsupervised approach that utilizes DNA sequences alone to extract essential features. A key component of our solution involves transforming DNA sequences into a continuous vector of real numbers, enabling their use as input to neural networks. By employing deep learning techniques in the unsupervised setting, we can automatically discover the optimal feature representation without any labeled data. The performance of our method is evaluated through task-specific assessments, demonstrating that this method can discover both biologically significant features and enhance prediction accuracy. Furthermore, we have also discovered that these features are robust and transferable, which could potentially be applied across various genomic prediction models.

The impact of surface modification on the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$(0001) ultrathin films was studied using various techniques, including growth, spectroscopy, and transport measurements. Our results show that films grown on a V(001) substrate exhibit repeated metal-insulator transitions, whereas those grown on a Pt(111) buffer layer do not exhibit this behavior. Using V K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy, we observed that both insulating V$_2$O$_3$ and metallic V$_2$O$_3$ have similar core-to-absorbed electron occupation probabilities, confirming that surface modification does not affect the chemical structure. Our findings are consistent with prior research on metallic V$_2$O$_3$(0001) films grown on insulating substrates. Our study demonstrates that by manipulating the surface modification, it is possible to induce the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$(0001) ultrathin films. Moreover, we observed that repeated transitions cause the films to become increasingly metallic, likely due to the accumulation of vanadium vacancies, underscoring the importance of understanding the effects of repeated phase cycling on the crystal structure.

The Clebsch canonical form for systems with Lie-Poisson brackets has been formally derived and characterized. For specific cases such as rigid body motion, it corresponds to the dual space of a Lie algebra, which in this instance is equivalent to the space of angular momenta. An essential benefit of the Lie-Poisson structure, which applies generally, is its capacity to reduce these momenta by the necessary number. This general approach was applied to various systems, including those of rigid and elastic bodies in two and five-dimensional spaces. An elastic body's angular momentum space was studied as a primary area. Additionally, it was shown that the general theory of Poincaré-Bendixson for Lie-Poisson structures can be applied to systems of Euler equations derived from their Hamiltonian density. Furthermore, it was proposed that a change in coordinates, which involves the use of a Lie-Poisson structure, could be used to express systems in the Clebsch canonical form. An example was given using the Euler equations for a fluid.

Using the data from the KMTNet system, we conducted a thorough analysis of all known extra-solar planets that were monitored in 2018. Out of a total of 47 planets studied, we identified 31 planets with anomalies, which means about 66% of the planets showed signs of being more massive than the typical Jupiter-analog planets. We discovered that planets with mass less than 1.5 times that of Jupiter tend to have longer orbital periods than their more massive counterparts, which could be attributed to a process called Type I migration. Additionally, we found that planets with mass less than 1. stellar mass exhibit a higher tendency to be located further away from their stars. Furthermore, we found that planets with mass greater than 1.5-2.5 times the mass of Jupiter tend to have shorter eccentricity and migration. Furthermore, we found that the distribution of eccentricity peaks at an eccentricity value of 0.3, which is lower than the overall eccentricity peak of 0.4 observed in the full KMTNet sample, indicating that planets in multiple star systems tend to have lower eccentricity.

A significant number of partial differential equations that describe conservation laws incorporate certain symmetries, leading to conserved quantities, often referred to as first integrals. We introduce an innovative approach to control these conservation principles within a particular class of equations that includes the compressible Navier-Stokes equations as a subset. This involves converting the specified conservation laws into unique restrictions on differential invariants, enabling control over these principles by restricting the space of invariants. As a particular example, we apply this method to the conservation of mass in a compressible, isentropic flow governed by Navier-Stokes equations and demonstrate its reduction to a particular condition on the divergence of the velocity invariants. Our method holds potential for application in various engineering and physical fields.

A prominent issue in the banking sector revolves around the management of non-performing loan assets. These loans have failed to generate revenue for banks due to payment difficulties on the part of borrowers. Effective classification of these loans is crucial for banks, enabling them to develop tailored recovery strategies and increase loan recovery rates. This research employs a real-life loan dataset to apply machine learning models for classifying loans. It involves analyzing and comparing machine learning models to identify the most suitable method for loan classification. Furthermore, this research utilizes the SHAP method to identify the most significant attributes influencing the loan classification process.

We introduce a new set of Dyck trails, a modification of the traditional Dyck paths, and find that their chromatic symmetric functions align with the existing frameworks of q-permutations and q-rooks. The concept of q-length is re-examined, revealing its equivalence to the chromatic number minus 1. Additionally, the symmetry and unimodality of these functions are explored, and several new identities are discovered.

Convolutional networks are highly effective at image recognition, but they often struggle with identifying images in the wild. To address this, we suggest incorporating orientation and disorientation into network layers, enabling them to interpret image directions consistently. By doing so, we developed the first direction convolutional network capable of processing images in various orientations. This enables the application of orientation-aware filters, making our model more robust and efficient. Furthermore, we created a new, simple optimization technique for sparse directed graphs and used it to develop a new layer type, reducing the computational requirements for handling images in various orientations. On the CIFAR-10 dataset, we achieved 94.4% accuracy with our model, demonstrating a 1.3% improvement over the standard convolutional network, while reducing computations by 2.5x.

We are solving a long-standing problem introduced by B. Gross, relating to a family of algebraic curves defined by Hecke groups, and proving that periods on them transcendental in nature. The proof relies on a modified version of a mathematical formula that compares representations, specifically one based on a group called USp(2,n), and its action on a space defined by the unimodular lattice Z^{2,n}. The core of the proof involves establishing an equality between terms in this formula, and its application extends to determine curvature of a key representation in a related context.

An investigation is conducted on the substantial flavor dependence of the top quark mass within the context of the Standard model, specifically focusing on the renormalization group evolution of its mass. This study reveals that light quarks significantly impact the top quark mass due to their substantial and distinct contribution to the beta function of the QCD beta function at one loop. As a result, there is a significant discrepancy between the top quark mass defined in the $\overline{\rm MS}$ and $\overline{\rm DR}$ schemes. Furthermore, it is shown that the presence of light quarks significantly alters the top quark pole mass by modifying the light quark vacuum energy. Furthermore, an analysis of the Wilson coefficient of the relevant operator in the weak interaction Lagrangian demonstrates that the effect extends to the matching condition between effective field theories and the Standard model.

We focus on $\chi$-boundedness issues related to the edge-choosability of subgraph restrictions on $K_r$-free graphs with a specific structure. Our main finding is that, given a structure $H$ (where $H$ is an $\{K_r, odd cycle\}$-free graph for some $r \geq 3$) and $\epsilon > 0$, there exists a corresponding choice number $q(H,\epsilon)$, which serves as a limit for $\epsilon$-almost regular graphs. This limit holds for graphs that are both $H$-structure and $\epsilon$-almost regular, which are subgraph restrictions on general graphs without $K_r$.

We establish a hypercontractive inequality in the context of a weighted Bernoulli space with an additional condition. This new inequality expands upon the work of Gross, Nielsen, and Extremal Functions Research Group's findings. Furthermore, this result facilitates the creation of concentration inequalities for Lipschitz functions defined on the space and provides an alternative proof for a recent inequality found by Extremal Functions Research Group.

A novel framework is introduced for analyzing low-dose COVID-19 CT scans, which are obtained through a two-stage process where the first stage involves reducing dose by lowering tube current and time, and the second stage employs deep learning to enhance these reduced-dose images using a noise reduction algorithm. A time-distributed capsule network is utilized in this research to effectively capture the spatial-temporal relationships within low-dose images and reduce computational complexity while maintaining high accuracy. To further enhance performance, a spatial attention mechanism is incorporated to focus the network on detecting COVID-19 lesions within low-dose images. As an application, a lung disease detection system is developed using this research. A dataset of 1,200 images is collected from the literature, which is then used to train and evaluate the proposed model. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed model achieves an average classification accuracy of 96.08% on COVID-19 cases, representing a significant improvement over state-of-the-art models.

The growing use of space-based services, like Earth observation and satellite communication, necessitates well-planned utilization of the space surrounding Earth. To meet these needs, a comprehensive planning framework is needed, involving the coordination of space-based services and their operators. This paper offers a detailed analysis of the space surrounding Earth in low-Earth orbit, followed by a designed space planning framework.

We've devised an innovative method for automatically creating high-quality, coarse quadrilateral meshes on CAD models by utilizing integer linear programming algorithms. These mesh generators come in two types: one that uses convex polygons and another that uses rotated squares. By implementing these algorithms in the Gurobi tool, we can efficiently optimize the meshing process. In contrast to traditional meshing techniques, we leverage the CAD model's geometric properties, such as face normals and symmetry, to refine quadrilateral features and improve the overall mesh quality. Our approach has been successfully tested on 100 complex CAD models, with the majority of edges falling within the recommended 10-25 size range. Furthermore, we allow users to adjust key parameters, such as the maximum number of quadrilateral features and the maximum distance between parallel lines, to suit different meshing needs.

The sample correlation coefficient offers a valuable method for examining relationships between variables. However, its evaluation through hypothesis testing and confidence intervals can be complicated due to non-normal distribution of its associated test statistic and the sample correlation itself, which depends on unknown population variances and covariances. This study aims to describe the probability density function of the sample correlation under all possible arrangements of the data, which is equivalent to considering sample correlations from datasets with samples of size n from k-dimensional normal populations, where the populations' covariance matrices have varying degrees of symmetry. By utilizing the notion of a sample correlation coefficient, this research also provides closed-form expressions for its expected value and variance for datasets of size n from k-dimensional normal populations, covering a range of symmetry levels for the populations' covariance matrices, and identifies expected values and variances for specific instances.

We propose an approach to solving Hamilton-Jacobi equations within the framework of General Relativity and similar frameworks. This method involves expanding the $S$ matrix in powers of the derivative using a suitable coordinate system. Each Hamilton-Jacobi equation is linked to a $S$ matrix, resulting in a set of shell equations. These equations are shown to be equivalent to the Schrodinger equation in a form with vanishing derivative terms. We apply this method to various potentials, including those of Liouville type. Additionally, we investigate the feasibility of constructing the inverse $S$ matrix for derivative terms in the Hamilton-Jacobi equation using the star product approach.

This paper presents a universal stabilization strategy for solutions of the 3D and 4D Navier-Stokes equations in both periodic domains and whole space, employing finite, localized interior feedback controls with the following key features:  1) the control mechanism is independent of the initial condition,  2) it is unaffected by the state variable,  3) the use of Sobolev and Besov space-based function spaces, and  4) the approach is applicable to both 3D and 4 dimensions of flow. Our approach involves working in critical Sobolev and Besov space settings to derive precise estimates for the decay rates of the external Laplacian, ultimately enabling the solution to decay in strong Sobolev spaces under diverse spatial dimensions and dimensions of flow.

Literature and historical figures' written words require contextual understanding through lexicons. Although some contextual dictionaries exist, they primarily serve literary purposes, making them less suitable for linguistic research. This paper introduces LitMind Lexicon, a publicly accessible digital dictionary accessible online at litmind.org. Underlying research and development are detailed, and the lexicographer's database is stored in MongoDB. Each dictionary entry contains word definitions, synonyms, and usage examples from literary sources. Users can submit new words, leading to ongoing lexicographical expansion.

The LIME framework, originally created for machine learning transparency, has been adapted for recommendation transparency, yet like its original application, LIME-RIME explanations can be difficult to understand and unreliable. This study builds upon the work of [2] by investigating two aspects of LIME-RIMEX explanations: local accuracy and reliability. To examine these factors, we derived key properties for LIME-RIMEX explanations and tailored them specifically for recommendation transparency, which involved adapting features used in LIME to a recommendation system and adjusting the feature weighting process locally around an item using similar items. The findings indicate that the choice of parameters and explanation methods significantly impacts the properties of the explanations generated by LIME-RIMEX, and the integration of neighbor items has a significant effect on the adherence of the explanations generated by LIME-RIMEX compared to those generated by LIME in prior studies.

Researchers have developed and experimentally validated a technique to modify the density of a specific type of quantum well, with the goal of adjusting the level where electrons settle within the well. By controlling the concentration of a different material during the quantum well creation process, the researchers adjusted the well's distance from a specific energy point, which helped adjust the level where electrons settle within the well. As a result, the researchers adjusted the gap in the well from 0.34 micrometers to 0.64 micrometers, which changed the level where electrons settled from 24% to 52% of the distance between the two energy extremes. This discovery has significant implications for the design of advanced quantum devices.

This study explores the robustness of learning under adversarial noise. The setting involves a learner receiving corrupted data from a distribution, where an adversary selectively corrupts a certain fraction of the data. The learner has the option to either accept an example as is or request an "local inspection" to verify its integrity. The learner must then make predictions based on the original or verified sample. The study examines under which concepts the learner can still make accurate predictions, even after being tricked by the adversary. The results identify the area of concepts for which local inspections are a necessary condition, as well as a broader class of areas where this condition can be achieved through specific parameters. The study also reformulates the necessary condition in terms of the underlying metric space of the concepts.

A key problem in optimal transport theory involves minimizing the cost between probability distributions $\mu$ and $\nu$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, characterized by parameters $d$ and $n$. Research into this issue, known as Fast Sinkhorn, has been ongoing, with the goal of developing efficient algorithms to compute optimal transport. Our research, referred to as Fast Sinkhorn II, presents a novel approach to precisely and efficiently compute optimal transport for a broad range of problems, leveraging a triangular matrix, $A$, and its fast collinear properties, all while maintaining a per-element operation complexity of $O(n^2/d)$. Our algorithm achieves this efficiency by employing an $O(n/d)$ size matrix $A$ to represent $T$ within $O(n/d)$ operations, thereby significantly reducing memory usage. Our approach is validated through performance benchmarks, demonstrating improvements over state-of-the-art methods for problems with $d > 1$.

AU Mic, a young M8V binary system, has a close-in planet c and potential planet b. Studies on the star's activity in the FUV have been conducted using NASA's Hubble Space Telescope. The research found no FUV activity during quiet periods but detected two FUV flares. The flares had durations and peak intensities. The findings suggest that AU Mic's FUV flares are less intense than in the optical band. The data also imply that AU Mic b and c receive significant FUV radiation. The results are also discussed in terms of the star's activity levels and the effects on the planets.

A non-conservative medium moving at constant speed through a collisionless dielectric medium creates intriguing radiation effects. This setup can be likened to the radiation produced by an accelerated charge, given a particular arrangement of the two scenarios. By focusing on the radiation emitted from a point charge moving perpendicularly through a unidirectional anisotropic medium, we can derive general expressions describing the energy loss due to radiation. Subsequently, we calculate these expressions for a circular trajectory and compare the results to established benchmark results when the medium is highly conductive.

In the realm of machine learning, handling class imbalance is a significant challenge. Many standard classifiers, including k-NN, tend to slightly favor the majority class. This class imbalance issue is particularly severe when employing the k-NN algorithm with an even value for k, as the vote-counting approach consistently grants the majority class an additional vote. This paper proposes a class imbalance-robust variant of the 2-NN algorithm and a-NN algorithm (where a is an even value), which are capable of yielding better results than the conventional k-NN in scenarios with class imbalance. The proposed variants are evaluated and compared against established classifiers and variations of k-NN, including lau-2-NN, as well as the a-NN algorithm. The evaluation is conducted on four well-known datasets, including the Pima Indians Diabetes, Arrhythmia, Credit-German, and Pima3 datasets. The results demonstrate that the proposed variants outperform the conventional k-NN algorithm, the laud-2-NN algorithm, and the one-class SVM in handling the class imbalance issue, while the laud-2-NN algorithm yields state-of-the-art performance on some datasets.

We have identified 13 new, distant quasars, detected through spectroscopy of the SkyMapper survey, spanning a redshift range of $z=2.5$ to $z=4.8$. These quasars, which possess luminosities of $M_{1450W} > -26.5$, significantly contribute to understanding the quasar luminosity function, particularly at high luminosities and redshifts. Our combined dataset, along with existing literature, reveals that $>90\%$ of quasars with luminosities of $M_{1450W} > -26.5$ are located beyond a redshift of $z=2$. Furthermore, this sample contains the most luminous, distant quasars known, with the most luminous having a luminosity of $M_{1450W}=-26.78$ at a redshift of $z=3.82$. A statistical analysis of our population indicates that $>90\%$ of the most luminous, distant quasars are hosted by galaxies with a mass of $>10^{11}M_{\odot}$.

We've developed a precise technique for probing the charge-tunneling dynamics of a quantum dot and superconducting island system. By carefully analyzing how electric charges move between these components in response to rapid changes in the dot's energy, we discovered that increasing the strength of the superconducting coupling significantly reduces the effective charge that can tunnel across the barrier. This phenomenon is attributed to the interference between different charge states within the island, which suppresses the higher-energy transitions more than expected. Our findings have been validated through detailed numerical simulations of the system's dynamics and have been compared with experimental measurements of charge tunneling.

We analyze and test the contraction property for systems of conservation laws that involve entropic discontinuities, focusing on the accuracy of numerical solutions. This investigation utilizes the Kruškov entropy-entropy flux pairs as a criterion for contraction, which are commonly paired with Euler equations to model phenomena such as gas bubbles and droplets. Nucleation phenomena, in particular, are described as boundary initial value problems and treated as a special case. The entropic discontinuity is characterized by a positive entropy jump, and we provide a physical interpretation of the resulting contraction property, including contraction in the $L^1$ norm of density and velocity differences, as well as in the $\mathrm{VMD}$ norm of velocity differences. Furthermore, it is shown that the $L^1$ norm of density differences also exhibits a contraction property. These findings are supported by one and two-dimensional numerical experiments that verify the contraction property for a variety of scenarios.

Creating immersive 3D environments solely from a single image has been a significant challenge in the field of computer vision. The recent integration of conditional diffusion models has significantly improved progress in this area, enabling the generation of high-quality, photorealistic views from novel angles. The diffusion process typically involves a two-step sampling procedure that reversibly transforms Gaussian noise into a final image, often incorporating various image properties to enhance the results. To further refine these models, researchers have introduced multiple views, allowing for a more accurate understanding of 3D properties. To address the issue of single-view condition diffusion models producing inconsistent and unrealistic results, we have developed the application of condition-based diffusion models to single-view perpetual view generation, specifically introducing the DiffDreamer. The model combines several techniques, including adaptive noise, multi-view diffusion, and a novel view synthesis approach, to generate high-quality, photorealistic results. By leveraging conditional information and incorporating image properties, DiffDreamer produces highly accurate and realistic 3D environments from single images, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in terms of both visual quality and geometric consistency.

Industrial processes are often optimized through networked systems, connecting multiple processes over distance. To meet demand and ensure quality, these networks must be precisely controlled, with predictive control methods like Model Predictive Control (MPC) commonly employed. MPC relies on mathematical models to forecast process behavior, but their effectiveness is limited when process dynamics are complex and non-linear. MPC also faces challenges when dealing with stochastic processes, like the spread of infectious diseases, where outcomes are uncertain and unpredictable. MPC's reliance on deterministic models restricts its utility in MPC applications. Our research presents a novel approach to address MPC limitations, using MPC alternatives that rely solely on data. Our approach uses a graph to analyze network processes, identifying relationships and dependencies between processes. Our method uses this information to build accurate process models, even in complex, non-linear systems, without relying on first-principles mathematical models. Our approach demonstrates the feasibility of using data-driven models for MPC, using the operation of power plants as a real-world example. Our approach also addresses MPC applications in complex, non-linear systems, where our framework can adapt and scale to meet the needs of various process configurations.

The behavior of a liquid layer on a cylindrical fibre was examined through both numerical and experimental approaches. This behavior is governed by the Rayleigh-Plateau instability, and we discovered that when there is significant slip at the liquid-solid interface, the instability's growth rate is enhanced, contrasting with the case where there is no such slip. This enhancement is most pronounced when there is no gravity, whereas under a downward gravitational force, we found that when the Bond number exceeds a certain threshold, the instability's growth rate is reduced as the liquid becomes more mobile, which is the opposite of what was expected. This new finding may explain the observation that under a downward gravitational force, higher capillary numbers can lead to the observation of longer undulations. Additionally, we proposed a theory that the energy dissipated by the instability is proportional to the square of the perturbation amplitude, and we showed that this theory is consistent with experimental results.

This investigation explores the Lipschitz stability of the Hunter-Saxton model, focusing on both its global and local solutions. By examining the underlying conservation laws, we find that it is possible to establish Lipschitz stability through local methods alone. Additionally, we investigate whether a similar approach is applicable to the Cauchy problem defined on a torus, and we develop a general procedure for creating stable representations of the solution, based on an arbitrary initial configuration of angles.

Evaluating scoliosis curvatures is typically done through ultrasonic imaging, which can be performed manually by a clinician, but this process lacks consistency and reliability. To address this issue, we propose a robotic system that uses ultrasonic imaging to assess scoliosis with greater reliability. Our system can detect the curvature of the spine and measure the angle associated with it, which in turn allows for the identification of the region of interest. Comparing our robot's performance with that of a human expert, we found that in 90% of the cases, the robot's measurement of the angle of curvature deviated by no more than 1.5 degrees from the expert's result. Furthermore, we developed a metric to quantify the reliability of the robot when interpreting the region of interest, which we believe surpasses the existing standards set by UL9609-1 for medical devices.

This paper introduces an method for creating synthetic speech of variable durations through a non-parametric approach derived from the given speaker's speech. The proposed technique relies on the assumption that the median synthetic speech duration closely matches that of the speaker. Initially, the proposed approach was tested on a small dataset of 50 speakers. Subsequently, it was applied to a larger group of 300 speakers to compare the perceived similarity of medium-length synthetic speeches with that of the actual speakers.

The rise of social media platforms has facilitated global interaction, but it has also enabled users to post anonymously, leading to the proliferation of hate speech which thrives on discriminatory content. As a result, there is a pressing need for automated hate speech detection. Existing studies have explored this by focusing on filtering inappropriate content at the content or transition level. This research introduces a novel approach, combining feature selection and deep learning-based techniques to identify hate speech at the sentence level. Specifically, we propose the Sequence Attention Bi-LSTM (SABLSTM) model, which is capable of extracting critical features from consecutive sub-units in consecutive sentences. Experimental findings indicate that our proposed feature selection method and SABLSTM model significantly outperform the baseline models on our established Indonesian social media dataset with a substantial 14% improvement.

In Multi-Input Multi-Output (MIMO) architectures, which aim to accelerate deep neural network training and inference, there is typically low utilization of the available Taps. This unused capacity is partially attributed to the lack of standardization in MIMO Taps usage. This study investigates how to implement shared feature sharing across MIMO Taps in Vision & Language models. Specifically, we explore the feasibility of incorporating global average pooling and global max pooling for shared feature sharing. Experimental results show that global average pooling preserves more information, while global max pooling yields more distinct and precise feature representations. Based on these findings, we propose a novel feature sharing strategy called Max Pooling then Average Pooling, which leverages the advantages of both average and max pooling. This approach is particularly effective in extracting multi-scale features, making it well-suited for complex Vision & Language tasks.

Historical manuscripts hold immense cultural and historical significance as they provide insights into the past through written texts, letters, and other forms of correspondence. These documents, often preserved in intricate illustrations, hold significant value across multiple disciplines, making the analysis of their content a significant challenge. Advances in computer vision and optical character recognition have made it possible to process the immense volume of these documents, with the analysis of available datasets being a crucial step in this direction. The analysis of datasets, including their size and structure, is essential to understand their limitations and the need for more comprehensive research. The paper presents a comprehensive survey of the most prominent historical manuscript datasets, highlighting their key features and limitations, and suggesting the use of these datasets in various applications, particularly in character and text recognition tasks.

To achieve precise low-speed control of high-speed systems like industrial robots, flatness-based control methods are highly effective. However, these systems possess inherent nonlinearity, which poses significant implementation challenges. To address this, we introduce an innovative approach utilizing secondary sensors to estimate joint positions and velocities at low speeds, enabling more accurate control. This strategy was successfully applied to an ABB IRB 1400 robot for fine motion applications, demonstrating improved control performance. Experimental results validate the proposed control scheme's efficacy, showcasing its potential for fine motion applications.

A study conducted on patients who experienced a myocardial infarction examined the effects of socioeconomic factors on their health outcomes, using a myeloid cell model. The research aimed to analyze recurrent time-to-event data by applying a statistical method suitable for identifying distinct patient subgroups based on the frequency and timing of events. Using a large Danish cohort, the study identified subgroups of patients experiencing myocardial infarction that differed in their event rates, event distributions, and risk of death. The results showed that socioeconomic factors such as education level and income had a significant impact on patients' health trajectories, with lower-income and less-educated patients experiencing more frequent events at earlier ages. The method utilized in this study demonstrated its potential to provide a comprehensive understanding of complex disease processes, while also highlighting the importance of considering individual patient characteristics and event histories in analysis.

The molecular continuum method is an efficient approach for large systems, as it uses a few key molecules to accurately represent numerous molecules. A major challenge in this approach is maintaining consistency between in-house and external software, especially when multiple molecules are involved. To address this, researchers have developed a novel method for integrating molecular calculations from different sources, overcoming inter-molecular consistency issues. This method was tested using the gas-phase electron affinity of ethane and ethene and the water dimer binding energy, and the results showed good agreement with experimental data and other established methods. This method has the potential to be used in the study of larger systems, such as the gas-phase electron affinity of larger alkanes and the benzoic acid dimer, further advancing the field of computational chemistry.

The vertices of a graph, when removed, leave no two unconnected vertices with a positive distance between them, a property that can be used to localize objects both inside and outside the graph, such as defects in semiconductor materials. The minimum number of vertices, removed, to achieve this localization, is called the metric dimension of the graph. Researchers have worked to determine the metric dimension of a graph, developing an efficient parameterized algorithm that exploits feedback vertex subsets and other structural parameters. The approach begins by removing key vertices, reducing the problem to analyzing the remaining components. The algorithm then iteratively identifies and removes a subset of vertices, each with a degree of freedom greater than a certain threshold. The removed subset's size and the threshold value determine the algorithm's computational complexity, which can be expressed as ${\mathcal{O}}^*(n^{\phi(1+\frac{1}{\tau})})$, where $\phi$ is the Golden ratio. The algorithm relies on previous work involving feedback vertex subsets and other structural parameters, such as feedback vertex minor and feedback vertex distance sum. The approach has been applied to develop parameterized algorithms for determining the metric dimension of a graph, with the first such algorithm using the feedback vertex distance sum parameter.

Inspired by mathematical frameworks like power frames, we develop a theoretical basis for topological structures defining directedness in higher dimensions, which has implications for modeling multi-dimensional directed systems in physics. A key aspect of this work involves introducing key concepts, power spaces, and defining the power framework, which is inherently associated with a power structure. We examine the power frameworks that correspond to $T_2$-topologies in various categories and establish conditions under which power structures are hereditary and inherit the property of being $T_2$. The paper also investigates the relationship between power structures and subspaces in different categories, establishing conditions under which power structures can be restricted to subspaces while retaining their properties.

This study focuses on the relationship between atmospheric water vapor and precipitation in the Earth's atmosphere. Since water is the primary source of precipitation, the air temperature and the availability of water vapor play a significant role in determining the precipitation levels. Previous research has shown that the atmospheric water vapor levels are directly influenced by the surface temperature, a phenomenon known as the Clausius-Clapeyron relation, and that this relationship is more pronounced in warmer climates and temperatures. In this study, we have used the CanESM2 climate model to simulate two distinct climate scenarios: a current climate and a hypothetical 'hot house' scenario, where the surface temperature is 3°C warmer. Our results indicate that the Clausius-Clapeyron relation holds true for current and warmer climates and leads to an increase in precipitation, with more intense precipitation events occurring at higher temperatures. Furthermore, our analysis reveals distinct patterns of precipitation among different types of weather systems, with tropical cyclones and frontal systems exhibiting the most significant precipitation increases.

We propose a method for constructing integrable, higher-spin versions of self-dual Yang-Mills theory. It relies on a twistor transformation, similar in nature to the original Cremononikolov map. This new approach extends the spin count while preserving the twistor integrability method. In the process, it also yields a simpler, equivalent case that mirrors the original map.

Deep learning models have achieved remarkable results in diagnostic medical image classification. However, the effectiveness of these models is severely compromised by noisy labels. Current noise mitigation methods rely on large datasets, limiting their application in the medical field due to concerns over patient privacy. We introduce a novel approach called Bayesian Statistics Guided Label Rejuvenation Mechanism (BSG-LRM) designed to address this limitation. This innovative method utilizes Bayesian statistics to minimize the impact of label noise during the training process, thereby enhancing the accuracy and robustness of deep learning models even in the absence of noisy images. Extensive experiments conducted on both public and self-collected datasets demonstrate that BSG-LRM significantly outperforms existing techniques in the medical image classification domain.

This study aims to find a projector that is both efficient and easy to calculate, with an optimal norm for the standard $L^p$ space, where $1\leq p\leq\infty$, on the interval $[a,b]$. By utilizing a specific interpolation method that involves exponential functions, we can approximate any function with a certain degree of continuity. Building upon a previously established framework, we derive an expression for the norm of the interpolation projector. Utilizing Bishop's Theorem, we establish that the norm of the interpolation projector exceeds $2$ and provide a method to determine its precise value for a given function. We also explore how to calculate its maximum possible value (the sharp bound) for any given function.

An associated random walk is introduced on a graph, incorporating additional parameters related to a graph automorphism's irreducible components, and a characteristic polynomial for the transition probability matrix is derived, as well as a determination of the walk's period.

A formal holistic specification of real-time systems requires precise mathematical definitions for timing constraints to be expressed in the Higher-Order Logic of Classical Higher-Order Logic. Timing constraints are typically represented using inequalities in temporal domains, but the addition of equality to these constraints presents a significant challenge in Classical Higher-Order Logic. To address this issue, we propose a new inequality/equality axioms system for real-time domains and illustrate its applicability with practical examples from traffic control, transceivers, and a real-time garbage collector. Furthermore, we developed a Sledgehammer verification procedure that automatically derives this new axiomatic system from an initial specification, leveraging the capabilities of Isabelle/Isar.

To efficiently simulate complex wall turbulence, researchers have developed coarse-grained, coarse-grained structure-based models. These models rely on structural similarities to describe the behavior of turbulence. A combination of this coarse-grained approach with machine learning techniques is explored to enhance the prediction of wall turbulence. By integrating the coarse-grained structure-based model with machine learning, the resulting model can more accurately predict turbulence characteristics. A specific machine learning model, which combines the coarse-grained structure-based model with a deep convolutional neural network, is tested and shows improved performance. The resulting model demonstrates better agreement with high-resolution turbulence data and accurately captures the behavior of wall turbulence. The proposed model offers a computationally efficient and accurate tool for studying wall turbulence.

We demonstrate the existence of self-dual solitons within a specific model that combines Born-Infeld and Skyrme elements, which are born in a four-dimensional space with topological charge $N$. These solitons possess a self-dual property where the potential energy equals the total energy density. Furthermore, we develop two distinct methods for proving the existence of these solitons: a variational minimization approach under specific constraints and a gradient flow approach. Both methods successfully find the potential energy of the solitons in a three-dimensional space as a function of $N$.

A new Weyl metal state, which breaks time-reversal symmetry but preserves particle-hole symmetry, has been found in the Hofstadter regime. The emergence of this state, specifically its Weyl nodes, is due to its charge-neutral nature, which circumvents constraints that link loops of Fermi surfaces to topological nodal lines. Studies have shown its presence in models based on honeycomb and triangular lattices under moderate magnetic fields, and two key characteristics were identified: the conversion of topological charges on Fermi surfaces into Weyl nodes and the localization of a system with a non-zero Chern number into nodal lines when its total Chern number is zero. The time-reversal-broken Weyl metal can be realized experimentally using ultra-flat band materials under magnetic fields.

This research proposes a hybrid nanoantenna design that efficiently converts quantum dots into nanolasers with high brightness and directionality. The innovative approach combines two types of metal nanopillars, one made of gold and the other of silicon, arranged in a specific configuration. By introducing a single quantum dot along the central axis of this structure, it resonantly enhances light emission through spontaneous coupling. Our numerical simulations confirm that the resulting photon source exhibits exceptional properties, including high brightness (approximately 10^7 W/cm^2), near-perfect directionality, and tunable emission wavelengths. The findings of this study lay the groundwork for further exploration of nanolasers based on similar hybrid antenna designs.

The phenomenon referred to as "anomalous screening" occurs in a mixture of small and large particles when the small particles are undercompacted. As a result of this effect, the small particles exert increased pressure on the large particles that are part of the solid phase, causing the large particles' scaffolding to collapse. This allows the small particles to displace the large particles and occupy more space within the mixture. Previous research has utilized continuum models to investigate the mechanism behind anomalous screening. However, the accuracy of these models remains unverified. In an effort to confirm the theoretical models, an experiment was conducted. The experiment. involved an arrangement of spherical beads with two distinct sizes that were placed within a rectangular container. The small beads. were released from the top and allowed to settle to the bottom. The experiment. found. the simulated and measured heights of the transition layer to be nearly identical. Furthermore. the measured and predicted pressure distributions within the transition layer also matched. The experiment. has significant implications. the findings. support the accuracy of the continuum models used to describe anomalous screening phenomena.

Utilizing advanced first-principles calculations, our research focuses on the electronic properties of a silicene substrate as well as its configuration when one-sided or in a central position with Mn atoms. We discovered that silicene exhibits metallic properties when adsorbed to hBN. When Mn is adsorbed to the top surface, it generates a 0.5 eV bandgap in the density of states (DOS) due to the splitting of a single d orbital, which also develops magnetism. When adsorbed in the center, it generates a 1.2 eV bandgap in DOS, which also displays magnetism. We investigated the potential applications of Mn adsorbed silicene in spintronic devices.

A significant portion of the energy from SNae is believed to be channeled into the surrounding interstellar medium, a concept that is supported by our current understanding of Sgr A*. The Sgr A East remnant, a key component of this theory, is thought to be the result of the supernova event that preceded it. The origin and precise location of remnant formation within Sgr A* remain uncertain. Our research suggests that Sgr A East likely developed as a supernova explosion approximately 10 parsecs south-west of Sgr A* at the centre of the galaxy. The supernova explosion theory that best matches our findings proposes a Type II supernova with a type Ia supernova as an alternative option. The formation of Sgr A East within Sgr A* can be explained by the supernova explosion's shockwave interacting with the dense, clumpy molecular clouds that were present in the Sgr A* environment.

Text classification systems face challenges when dealing with imbalanced data, where some categories are underrepresented. To address this issue, researchers have developed various data augmentation methods, including COPY, FORGET, MASK, and a proposed technique called SYN. These techniques are designed to analyze the similarities between text entries and create more balanced data sets. Our study compares the effectiveness of these augmentation methods in multi-class text classification, and the results show that SYN outperforms COPY, MASK, and even COPY in most cases. Furthermore, we found that combining all the methods along with SYN yields the best accuracy, and the best machine learning model achieved an 80.7% accuracy on the 20 Newsgroups dataset. To replicate our findings, the code and data are available for download.

This study provides the first comprehensive, year-long analysis of local news coverage and audience engagement in the U.S. during the COVID-19 pandemic. Notably, one-third of U.S. residents receive news from local TV or online sources. We created an innovative dataset combining one year's worth of pandemic-related local news articles and audience engagement data from 3,162 markets. Our research found that local news outlets covered the U.S. COVID-19 crisis 10 times more than national outlets on average. We also found significant variations in coverage by region, with the South having the lowest amounts of pandemic coverage. Furthermore, our findings are consistent with an underlying 'information cascade,' with more pandemic exposure leading to higher testing and case numbers. We found a strong correlation between pandemic news coverage and U.S. COVID-19 cases and deaths. We found a significant 'information cascade' in pandemic news coverage, with more pandemic exposure leading to higher testing and case numbers.
